speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN EASTERN DOMESTIC PRICE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and1 Commerce with reference to the statement he made when he announced an increase of 30 cents per bushel basis Fort William for western domestic wheat. Will the minister give consideration to the necessity of removing the present discrimination by a corresponding increase in the price of eastern domestic wheat?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN EASTERN DOMESTIC PRICE
speechtext: I do not admit at all that there is any discrimination between the price paid in the east and in the west. The eastern wheat grower is paid basis Montreal, $1.40 per bushel. The western grower receives an initial payment of $1.35 a bushel basis Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. That is an advance. During the crop year 1946-47 the Ontario wheat producers received the following payments: ceiling price basis Montreal S1.26; treasury payment, S0.09; wheat flour equalization payment $0.05, making a total of $1.40 a bushel. This basis became effective on July 1, 1946 and will expire on June 30, 1947. There is very little Ontario wheat still remaining in the hands of the producers.

On the orders of the day:
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): I should like to ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply a question as to the outlook for supplies of domestic fuel oil, particularly in the light of the reports of refusal of some of the companies to supply consumers who have not bought their equipment from them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recall that coal control and the control of petroleum products were abolished at the end of the year, so that the matter to which he refers is not now in my immediate province. At the end of the year, while it was becoming apparent that the demand for fuel oil had been underestimated, the situation indicated an equitable distribution of available supplies.
As early as June of last year I called all the oil distributors into conference and urged them to examine the requirements for fuel and to make adequate provisions for taking care of these requirements. I also called together the producers of oil burners and asked them to state their needs and to meet with the distributors of oil to make sure that each understood the position of the other. A committee of the oil producers was formed, and I continued to correspond with them for several months. I received a definite assurance that supplies of crude oil had been purchased which would take care of the situation this winter. As part of the arrangement I provided priorities on steel for extra tankage and for distributing tank wagons. It seemed up to the end of the year that provision for meeting the fuel oil situation had been adequate.
I have traced down several accusations that oil companies will not take care of equipment sold by others. I found them entirely groundless. I think the situation is that the oil companies have contracted for all the fuel oil they are able to supply for the remainder 
of this season and are not able to take care of new installations whether by themselves or by others. That is as I follow the situation without having any special responsibility for it. I doubt very much whether my hon. friend can substantiate the accusation that the leading distributors of oil are treating the installers of oil burners in a discriminatory way.
On the orders of the day:

This matter is under consideration, and I hope to give my hon. friend a reply tomorrow.
On the orders of the day:

May I direct a question to the Minister of Transport? In view of the closing down of certain industries and the threat of the closing down of others because of the lack of rolling stock to move freight, will the minister make a statement on the situation?

The position with reference to
rolling equipment of the railways at the moment is acute, owing to the shortage of box cars and the large demands of those requiring wheat in western Canada, feed for the east, the requirements of pulp and paper industry and many other commodities. The transport controller, in conjunction with the railways, has given instructions to distribute box cars as equitably as possible among the various commodities, and is doing his very best to see that no industries will close down in the emergency. I can assure my hon. friend that every effort is being made to meet the conditions as they arise.

May I ask a supplementary question? Has the minister been able to make arrangements with certain railways of the United States?

On the orders of the day:
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Owing to the publicity in the newspapers of the maritime provinces with respect to Prince Edward Island, one of the nine provinces of Canada, this province is the only one not represented on the redistribution committee. I am not asking for representation on it myself, but 1 certainly think that our province should be recognized by representation on the committee.

The house resumed from Tuesday, February 18, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act and to make provision for matters presently provided for by regulation under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1915, including provision for the guarantee by the Minister of Finance of loans made to the Canadian wheat board on security of grain acquired by the Canadian wheat board and the payment of other expenses incidental to the operations of the board.

The question before us is simple, clear-cut and deserving of a straightforward answer. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act and to make provision for matters presently provided for by regulation under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, including provision for the guarantee by the Minister of Finance of loans made to the Canadian wheat board on security of grain acquired by the Canadian wheat board and the payment of other expenses incidental to the operations of the board.
Surely no hon. member will oppose the adoption of that resolution.
Even the leader of the opposition, speaking to this resolution on Tuesday, February 18. stated-and I quote from page 575 of Hansard:
At the moment I am not going to oppose any of the principles of this measure, but I do think the members of the house should know, and I think the Canadian people should know, something about what has been done by this board in recent months in order that we may be in a better position to decide what powers shall be entrusted to it in the future.
CMr. Speaker.]
Then he proceeded to place on the record a whole list of questions to which he demanded an answer before he would even consider the bill which is to follow this resolution.
In my opinion many of those questions should have 'been placed on the order paper, or been asked at some more appropriate time. Surely that great party that used to be known as the Conservative party has not become so bankrupt of ideas and leadership that this represents their official stand on such an important question. If it is, then may I suggest that they should have used the word "regressive" instead of "progressive" when they added that prefix to their name.
On page 578 the hon. the leader of the opposition stated, and I quote:
There are two other questions. One has to do with the -wheat agreement in its relation to the expansion of trade, in its relation to what is spoken of as multilateral trade. In a few months Canada will be joining with some twenty-six nations in Geneva to begin negotiations to restore the widest possible measure of international trade, to try to increase our trade. 1 should like to ask the minister or the prime minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) if they do not think the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement makes more difficult of accomplishment the international trade organization proposals for expanding multilateral trade.
Throughout his address the leader of the opposition proceeded to cast veiled criticisms and questioned the advisability of continuing the wheat board as it is operated at present; yet at no time did he make a definite statement as to which side of the fence he and the Conservative party were on.
At the beginning of my remarks I stated that the question before us was simple and deserving of a straightforward answer. Now I should like on behalf of our C.C.F. group to place our stand on record.
1.	We are unanimously in favour of the wheat board continuing to be the sole marketing agency of our wheat. I will go even further than that and say that we desire flax and all coarse grains to be included under the act.
2.	Unless the bill which is to be brought down has in it some new principle not forecast in the resolution, we see no need to send it to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
3.	We will exercise our right to criticize any undesirable features that may be incorporated in the bill, and may even offer amendments in committee of the whole to help make it a better piece of legislation.
Permit me to deal briefly with the three points I have just enumerated. I shall speak on the third first, because we feel that the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
details of this bill cannot properly be discussed until we are in the committee of the whole; and while we contend that there may be many imperfections in the act as it is at the present time, yet they do not constitute any fundamental part of this resolution or bill.
Dealing with number two, we see no need of sending this bill to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. This question of a wheat board and all that it means to the producers of this country has been so fully discussed in the past twenty-five years that the time has surely arrived when we must realize that it has been settled.
Consequently there is no need to worry you, Mr. Speaker, or other hon. members with lengthy quotations from authoritative sources. By this time the lines have been distinctly drawn between the great majority of producers on the one hand who claim that it is in the national interest that gambling in the foodstuffs of the nation should no longer be tolerated, and, on the other hand, those who believe that they have an inalienable right to exploit the marketing machinery of this country to the detriment of both the producer and consumer.
Here let me say that we at all times advocate that those who do the physical handling of our grain should have a fair and decent compensation for their services, but in our opinion that is all that they are entitled to.
As to the first point, concerning the continuation of the wheat board as our sole marketing agency, I may say that there again the lines have been distinctly drawn between those who exploit the farmer and the consumer on the one hand and the majority of the producers on the other. Among that group of producers there are many who see good in the wheat agreement signed with Britain, especially the long-term feature of that agreement and the stability it may bring; and regardless of the imperfections that there may be in the wheat board, they continue to support the board because only through it or a similar agency can that stability be assured.
I may say that these people are looking forward to the day when we shall have an agreement much more far-reaching in effect than the present one. Here I should like to thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce . (Mr. MacKinnon) for having tabled ' the memorandum on the proposed international wheat agreement before this discussion started. I am sure every hon. member will wish our delegates to that conference, which is to be held next month in London, England, every success.
May I draw the attention of the house to the fact that if and when an international wheat agreement is signed on our behalf, first of all it will supersede our present agreement with Britain, and, second, we shall have all the greater need for the wheat board to operate with all the powers it has at present. It is my duty to draw to the attention of the minister and his colleagues on the wheat committee of the cabinet the fact that there is an ever-increasing number of farmers who, while giving whole-hearted support to the wheat board, contend that regardless of what kind of agreement we have with other countries, our own internal price structure must be such that our farmers will at all times be assured of parity prices. In other words, they believe that the initial payment should be as near as possible to the price that the wheat board receives from the sale of our wheat under the present agreement; and then at the end of the year, a properly constituted fact-finding board, using the figures obtainable from the bureau of statistics, would decide what further payment was due to the farmers on their participation certificates, in order to bring their returns up to parity.
^ I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this word "parity" has been abused and misused; but all that these people are asking for is that the farmer be able to dispose of the products of his labour at a price which will give him the cost of production, and that he receive a fair share of the national income. May I appeal to the minister and his colleagues on the wheat committee of the cabinet to give earnest consideration to this question and endeavour at some time in the near future to bring in a bill which will satisfy these reasonable demands. In the meantime we-and I believe I express the wishes of the majority of producers-welcome this resolution and hope that we shall not need to wait too long before we obtain the other one.
May I also say that in supporting this resolution we are doing so not because we love the Liberal party and all its workings-it is not a question of supporting or opposing the government-but because we believe that the legislation forecast in this resolution is in the best interests of our country and the people who produce the foodstuffs of the nation, and believe that the powers granted to the wheat board under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act should be continued until we have something better to take its place.
Having stated the policy of our group, Mr. Speaker, I submit that this parliament and the people of this country are entitled to a more definite statement as to where the Progressive Conservative party stands on this

Canadian Wheat Board Act

important question. We shall see what the bill is, and if the bill is in line with what this resolution forecasts, we will help to pilot it through the house.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the proceedings it is not my intention to make a long speech, but on behalf of the Social Crediters I want to state now that we are in favour of the principle of the resolution. We are also in favour of the Canadian wheat board and feel that it should be continued in operation. This does not mean, of course-as we shall show later- that we are in favour of all of the wheat policy of the government. It is my intention, as well as that of my colleagues, to make our stand known on second reading and in committee, and to ask for improvements in the wheat policy of the government. This, I believe, is sufficient to show the house exactly where we stand, and we hope that speedy action will be taken with respect to this matter.

Mr. Speaker, there are some references that I intend to make to this resolution, some views that I wish to place before the house, and some questions that I desire to ask. I also wish to give support to the stand taken by the leader of this party that in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole-primarily of the farmers of western Canada but indeed of farmers in all parts of the country- this resolution and the bill founded thereon should be submitted to the committee on agriculture so that information may be available to the house and the country regarding the wheat question, in connection with which the government of the da37, through the instrumentality of the wheat board, is engaged in one of the greatest businesses in the Dominion of Canada.
Reference was made by my 'hon. friend of the C.C.F. party to the attitude taken by the leader of tihe opposition (Mr. Bracken). The leader of the opposition needs no defence on the part of any of his followers when the question of agriculture is being discussed here or anywhere else in Canada; for it was the leader of the opposition who in 1943 enunciated a policy on behalf of agriculture-
This is good.

If there are any questions I shall be glad to answer them at any time. Some hon. gentleman said, "This is good." Well, sir, it was a good policy that was enunciated by the leader of the opposition, and much of it has been borrowed by the government, for which we are thankful. The chattering has already commenced. We listened in silence while the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) was speaking-

.An hon. MEMBER: Reading his speech.

Well, in his case I call it speaking. Perhaps these interruptions might cease, unless questions are to be asked.
I was dealing with the attitude taken by the leader of the opposition, and as I look over his declarations made in 1943 the stand he took then has been followed not only by many individual members but sometimes by the government. Some of his expressions, such as "equality for agriculture" and "the assurance to agriculture of a fair share of the national income," together with his policies in regard to preventing a collapse of prices and 'the expansion of export markets, have been adopted in whole or in part. When my hon. friend, dealt in such fulsome terms with the resolution under which this government would take over not only all the wheat of the country but all the barley, all the oats and all the other farm products, he was being consistent, because in its policy the government is in fact carrying out the policy of my hon. friends to the left in socializing a large part of the production of one of the great industries of this dominion.
I was glad to hear the words of approval coming from my hon. friend. A similar system is in effect in England. I have here the British agriculture bill. I do not know the extent to which the government has followed this bill, but I would point out that in the explanatory memorandum issued by the minister of agriculture at the time this bill wras before the British House of Commons this statement was made in regard to agricultural policy:
The twin pillars upon which the^ governments agricultural policy rests are stability and era-ciency. The main method of providing stability is through guaranteed prices and assured irar kets, which are dealt with in part I of the bill.
To that there can be no objection. It goes on:
Part I provides, however, the necessary machinery which will enable the agricultural ministers to carry out periodical reviews of the general economic position and prospects of the industry, to fix prices to enable farmers to plan well ahead, and ... to promote measures to provide assured markets for the main agricultural commodities.
How does it say that can be achieved? Only by the socialization of the land of the United Kingdom, on the part of those who do not fall in line with the directions of the government. It goes on to say:
Stability, however, is not enough. It is equally important to ensure that the industry attains the highest possible degree of efficiency. In the government's view the state has both a duty and a right to see that the necessary steps are taken to this end.

Will the hon. member permit a question?
I am reading now.
You said you would answer questions.

My hon. friend never gets up to speak, much less to answer questions, but for the moment let me finish this quotation and then I shall be glad to answer the question.
One of the most important methods of promoting efficiency in agriculture is to ensure that farmers have made available to them the benefits of modern agricultural research, and knowledge of the most up-to-date farming methods.
Then it goes on to say-and I am not quoting at the moment-that in case there are farmers who will not do that, the government will have to take over the land.

The question I wished to ask the hon. member was this. Is he aware that the farmers' union in Great Britain, which has a membership of over ninety per cent of the land owners of that country, approved the British agriculture bill, and that it was also approved by the counterpart in Great Britain of the party which the hon. gentleman represents?

The latter statement is incorrect. The first statement is correct. Now I ask the hon. gentleman a question. Does he think that in order to assure efficiency on the part of farmers who are not as efficient as others, the proper system is first to give them warning that within one year they must farm efficiently, otherwise their land will be taken over by the state? Does he think that should be done?
The proper agricultural policy to follow in any country is the policy desired by the majority of the farmers in that country, and that is the policy that was followed in Great Britain.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that is the attitude of hon. gentlemen to my left. They believe in socialization for everyone else, but because of the number of farmers in this country they are very careful not to take such a stand in regard to agriculture. No one could have been fairer than I was in giving my hon. friend the opportunity to approve for Canada that of which he speaks in such fulsome terms as having been adopted in the old country. Only the other day-and I mention this in passing-an advertisement for a flour broker appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. It was worded in the following fashion:
Required immediately flour broker between exporter and flour mill for well-established export house; must be well acquainted with all large mills and have cordial relationship with wheat board.
I do not know why it was asked that the applicant should have cordial relationships with the wheat board. But that was the advertisement, in any event, and it causes one to stop and ask why.
A great many farmers in western Canada want to know why it is that the difference between the world price and the amount they are required to receive for their wheat under the British agreement is not being taken, up by the government of Canada as a whole, instead of the loss falling wholly on the farmers. They want to know why today the price on the Chicago market is approximately $2.40 while they receive 86 cents a bushel less for their wheat. They realize that on the basis of the present prices, having marketed or being about to complete the marketing of 330 million bushels of last year's crop, the farmers of Canada lost, under the present administration, approximately $280 million which, translated into the case of the average small farmer with 2,500 bushels, means that he has lost over $2,000. The farmers want to know why during the next four years they are entitled to receive only $1.35, and not $1.55, the approximate parity price referred to by the hon. member on my left.
They want to know whether the administration staff of the wheat board is efficient, totalling as it does, in strength, approximately 700 in Winnipeg alone. They want to know why during the past three years approximately 1,200,000 duplicate participation certificates remained unclaimed. They want to find out whether some efficient method cannot be devised of ascertaining the names of the holders of these certificates. Unless they are ascertained the wheat board and the country are going to have an overage running into millions of dollars.
I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the same system might be applied as was applied in 1931 or 1932, when the administration paid five cents a bushel to the producers of wheat. At that time there were many certificates which were not taken up, and the government of that day placed the matter in the hands of the pools and the other wheat agencies. Those agencies, equipped with bonds of indemnity, in a short time cleared up the problem. The total amount paid to the agencies for this service was 50

Canadian Wheat Board Act
cents a thousand. The attitude of the government, as evidenced apparently by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is that participation certificates cannot be paid because of these outstanding certificates.
I support in every particular the stand taken by my leader in regard to the necessity for the continuance of the wheat board, and that the time has come for an accounting so that we in parliament may find out how the moneys are being expended by the wheat board, and have the clear financial .picture of the board's business. It is not sufficient to give us a statement at the end of the year, encompassed in a compendium of fifteen or sixteen pages. We want particulars. We want the answers to the several questions to which I have already referred on behalf of the people of Canada. What has been the situation with respect to the wheat board? It has hidden behind governmental protection. One development in that connection was the Oatway case, wherein Mr. Oatway sued the board for a full accounting of its transactions between 1937 and 1942. That was a matter of interest throughout western Canada.
We want to know whether there was efficiency in the operation, whether proper principles are being adopted, and generally the entire set-up. Mr. Oatway started an action, and the government counsel, on behalf of the wheat board, raised the defence that the wheat board was an emanation of the crown and therefore could not be sued. The trial judge dismissed the application. An appeal was taken to the court of appeal of Manitoba, and the court held that proceedings against the wheat board could not be taken for an accounting. An appeal was then carried to the Supreme Court of Canada. Here was an individual asserting rights against the state, and what did the government do? Did they allow that individual to carry his appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada? They did not think it was sufficient to hide behind the defence that the wheat board was an emanation of the crown, so they passed an order in council denying anyone the right to ask for an accounting from the wheat board. If that is not autocracy, I ask what is? First they let a man go to the courts. Then they raise the defence of the state's freedom from action by the individual. Then fearing that that doctrine might not apply so far as the wheat board was concerned they hid behind the defence of an order in council passed and made retroactive in effect to deny the individual his right to his say in court.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I do not agree with it wherever it is done.

I knew the hon. member for Rosthern would not, because after all, while my hon. friend and I disagree in many things, in these matters concerning the supremacy of the state over the individual we have similar views. I only wish that the ideas of my hon. friend could find their way into and permeate the mind of the government.
The Progressive Conservative party asks that this matter be sent to the committee on agriculture. We ask for something more, that the wheat board coming before that committee will not hide as it did in 1942 and 1943; for when we asked for information that might prove embarrassing, the defence raised was that although they were perfectly willing to answer it was not in the public interest to answer. In war time that excuse went down, but today "it is not in the public interest" must no longer be a defence for bureaucrats who endeavour to do the business of the country under secrecy, surreptitiously, and free from the control of parliament.
I suggest that the board come before the committee on agriculture and place all their cards on the table; let the people know the extent to which, by reason of inefficiency, demurrage amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars has piled up on ships destined for Britain. Let this country know why it is that Canada has not carried out the agreement with the British people. We gave them cheap wheat because their food situation was serious, and no one criticizes that; but our attitude on this side of the house is that when charity is done by a nation the loss should fall on the nation itself, not on the farmers as producers in the nation.
The British people are starting to criticize. They want to know why they are not getting our wheat. Because, Mr. Speaker, you cannot feed hungry people with cheap wheat that is not shipped when it is needed. They want to know why it is that in order to meet the wheat situation Britain is purchasing from the United States wheat at about $3 a bushel, from the Argentine at $3.27 a bushel, from Turkey at $4.04. On the other hand the farmer in Canada wants to know why in face of the world situation with wheat selling at those prices he should be compelled to accept $1.35 a bushel paid now and then wait another four or five years for his participation certificates to mature. All over the west the farmer is asking for the payment of his participation certificates annually, that he shall not have to wait five years. He is asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is not in the house just now, to make provision immediately for the payment of the participation certificates for 1943 to 1945.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
The minister is out at the moment meeting the Minister of Food from Great Britain.

I thank my right hon. friend for mentioning that, because it is unfortunate that a debate on a matter so pertinent to the Department of Trade and Commerce should not have been postponed to an occasion when he could have been here.
He will be back in a few minutes.

I thank my right hon. friend for letting me know that.
The farmers want to know something about the barley and oats situation, to which reference was made a day or so ago by the Minister of Agriculture. They want to know what the prices are going to be. The price of wheat is to be fixed under the statute at $1.35 a bushel forthwith, and the farmers want to know what the prices of oats and barley will be. The price of oats the Canadian farmer receives is from twenty-five to fifty cents a bushel less than the price at which our farmers could sell it in other countries, and the price of barley fifty cents a bushel less. What is the minimum price going to be if the government takes over barley and oats? The farmers want to know the circumstances connected therewith; otherwise the government is asking for blanket statutory authority for the wheat board to do what it likes with respect to oats and barley. If barley and oats are to be taken over by the government as in war time, the farmer has a right to know the terms upon which he will produce and the prices which he will receive.
I have given three or four reasons why this matter should be sent to the committee. I believe, sir, that this is an opportunity for hon. members in all parts of the house to make a declaration on behalf of the membership of this house that the time has come to assert the right of parliament to full inquiry and explanation by bureaucrats who administer large businesses under the state. We have the right to full information; othewise we shall be approving the placing in the hands of three men the right to expend millions and billions of dollars free from supervision other than a report satisfactory to the Minister of Trade and Commerce which is to be given at the end of each year.
There are other reasons why this matter should come before parliament. I have already dealt with the national well being, the well being of the producers and processors and of the country as a whole who have the right to full information.
Parliament has the right to know what the position of the wheat board is today; for its character has changed since 1935 when the board was set up as an independent agency for the marketing of wheat. It was then instructed, not by the government, but by statute. That position has changed over the years so that today the wheat board is operating under order in council and by regulations which can be set aside in whole or in part by order in council. If British experience means anything the only way in which they can assure a marketing policy when taking over all farm products-and in this case we are taking over the major portion of the farm products-is by acreage control and delivery quotas plus utilization of the land in accordance with government direction.
When this government came into power it was in railroad transportation, in part in wheat, and in part in radio. Today it is in public information, in aviation, in rubber production. Finally this resolution places them in control of practically all the field crops of the country. This indicates the trend away from parliament, a trend toward a form of socialization the like of which we have not had before in this country.
To sum up, we want to find out why the prices have been fixed by the government below world values; why each farmer should be required to suffer a loss to the extent that I have already mentioned; why the whole policy in reference to the wheat board was changed from government by statute to government by order in council, apparently a practice to be perpetuated in the days of peace-for that is what parliament is being asked to do.
During war time parliament was prepared to go a long way. We abdicated our power; we were willing, we were ready, we were desirous of doing everything toward uniting the country. The bureaucracy which was built up in war time, however, is not desirous of releasing any part of its hold now that peace is here. In this bill parliament has an opportunity to review the whole situation. Hon. members irrespective of party have an opportunity to assert their independence. I am asking the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) to join in this. Hon. members have an opportunity to make government agencies responsible to parliament, to make them responsible to hon. members for whatever has been done, and in committee enable the board to give explanations for its policies and to make excuses where excuses are found necessary.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
We are in agreement with the resolution; we intend to give it our support. On the other hand we are asking that parliament be empowered to investigate. The hon. member for Humboldt said that his party was opposed .to having it sent to a committee. Naturally he took that view. That is the attitude of the government in power in Saskatchewan which is operating public corporations. They want to give a general summary only. They are not anxious to agree to a principle which in their own province-
On a point of order, at the last session the government of Saskatchewan offered to set up a committee, and I believe did set up a committee to investigate the matter.

They offered to do it. Offering to do a thing and doing it are two different things. They offered to do it, but they did not do it. They came out in blazing colours telling what profits they had made. The only reason they were able to show a profit at all was that they were not in the position of other private companies, of having to pay taxation within the province.
They do not elect any Tories either.

I cannot answer interruptions that I do not hear, as I have said before. I am pointing out the facts. That is the reason I can understand the attitude of my hon. friends to the left. If they were to support us in asking that this matter be sent to a committee of parliament some member in the small opposition in the legislature in Saskatchewan might rise in his place and say: How about having the accounts of these various corporations submitted to a committee of the legislature? They would then find themselves in a difficult position to explain, having taken one attitude here and another one there. I am asking hon. members in all parts of the house to support us in the stand taken by the leader of the opposition that the time has come to have crown corporations answerable to hon. members of the House of Commons and to the representatives of the people; for without that declaration hon. members will be giving their approbation to a state of affairs which we accepted in war time but which should not be perpetuated in the days of peace.

I wish to make a few observations on this resolution which says that it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
I wish first of all to support all the arguments made by my leader when he spoke on this resolution, and to endorse the questions which he asked' of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). Like those of my party who have spoken before me, I trust that after the second reading this measure will be referred to the agriculture committee. Surely after all that has happened these many years we are entitled to some information. It is many years since we have received an accounting from the Canadian wheat board.
A previous speaker referred to the Oatway case. The government passed an order in council which would not allow any further procedure in the courts to obtain information.
Speaking in the house on Tuesday evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that in many commodities the Canadian price level is now materially below the world price level. I am sure that there is agreement in that. As a result of direction and controls by this government, chiefly through the Canadian Wheat board, and based upon statistics for certain given years which I am going to quote from the Searle index report of August 21, 1946, the marketing of the Canadian wheat crop from the prairies in 1943 meant a loss to the producers of wheat in that year of $145 million, or an average of 44f cents a bushel. The marketing of the 1944 crop meant a loss of $139 million, or an average of 57| cents a bushel. The marketing of the 1945 wheat crop meant a loss of $110 million, or 5T6 cents a bushel.
May I be so bold as to predict that for the marketing of the 1946-47 crop, as a result of the United Kingdom agreement and our domestic agreements, we shall have a loss of at least $180 million. That is based on the average loss of 55 cents a bushel. In these first three years for which I have given the actual figures, the total loss was $394 million on wheat alone from the prairie provinces. That amount, added to the $180 million that I predict for this year, will make a loss of $574 million in the marketing of the wheat crop alone. Similar statistics could be given for coarse grains and for live stock on the same basis.
Remember that we are already over the seventh month in, the marketing of this year's crop. When the agreement with the United Kingdom was signed, before the commencement of this crop season, wheat was selling on the open market at $2.05 a bushel. The contract was signed at $1.55. The price of wheat has risen consistently from that day on. I think it was about $2.10 at the start of this season and has consistently risen until No. 2 Canadian wheat, that is export wheat,
6ib
Canadian Wheat Board Act

is quoted today at $2.47 a bushel. That is a great loss. Hon. members of this house and the people should bear that in mind, because if we are to take seriously the statements of economists that we are due for some recession then I do not know ihow these people are to be reimbursed for the great losses they have taken during these years.
Yesterday it was significant to hear the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), supported by another minister, say that there would be no subsidies on production in the future. True, he was talking about something else, but that was the general statement, and it is rather significant. I would remind the house that in 1945, the year prior to the signing of the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement, we in Canada exported in round figures 329 million bushels of wheat, and of that total some 113 million bushels were exported to the United Kingdom, the rest going to the various other countries-and we usually export wheat to 67 countries.
I do not think that the people of the country generally realize what the farmer receives net. While the contract price is SI.55, the wheat producer in the prairie provinces receives at point of delivery at the elevator less than $1.20 a bushel. It is quite true that he is given a participation certificate, but upon that certificate he may never receive anything.
Under the proposal which is to be included in the bill, these certificates are to be pooled until 1950. Every farmer in the west objects to this and thinks there should be a settlement annually on the certificates. The farmer may never receive any more than this sum of less than $1.20 a bushel. Certainly, on the basis of past experience some believe that he will receive a very negligible amount, if anything.
A week or so prior to the signing of the agreement last summer I received resolutions from farmers in my constituency. Farmers who signed the resolution were members of the Manitoba Pool Elevators Association and they asked that there be an initial payment of $1.80 on all wheat, whether for domestic use, for export or for other purposes.
Much is made of the statement which the Minister of Trade and Commerce made the other daj" on the price of wheat for domestic consumption in Canada. The newspapers carried headlines to the effect that this would mean slightly over $10 million for the farmers for the rest of the year, but they did not carry headlines, as they might have done, indicating that it had cost the farmers over $20 million annually ever since 1942, which is an unfair share of the burden of price stabilization. That is what they contributed to the price stabilization policy. This is not

retroactive. They have lost that every year from 1942 to this date, so that it is a step in the right direction.
Everyone knows that from the time the agreement was signed with Britain the cost of production has been rising daily. The bureau of statistics will point out that farm wages were at an all-time high last fall, and the farmer is the only man who is tied to such a condition today. The lumberman, the manufacturer of farm implements and others are exporting a great percentage of their output at prevailing world prices. All this adds to the cost of production. I am sure, as sure as I am standing here, that if the increase in freight rates now asked for by the railway companies is granted, or even a portion of that increase, it will add many millions of dollars to the cost of the prairie producer in marketing his wheat and other grains. That is another added cost that was never taken into consideration.
On the basis of the 55 cents a bushel loss that I have already given as my estimate, based on future markets, it may well be that we could provide the 160 million bushels annually for the first two years to Britain at a price of $2.10 a bushel, which is at least 35 cents below the present export prices, and then we could give to Britain, for nothing, 140 million bushels of wheat in the third and fourth year and be $50 million further ahead for the producer, less any extra that might be paid on participation certificates. That is the type of stability we have in that contract.
A great deal is made of stability. I realize that the Minister of Agriculture had a great deal to do with advising the Minister of Trade and Commerce with reference to the contract, and I am bound to say that in my opinion he has been very ill advised by leaders to whom he has a right to listen, some leaders in the federation of agriculture and in other important offices. When these people say that the farmers are all for this type of stability they have not taken into account the various consequences. They have ignored the rising cost of production generally and its effect on the production of this wheat. Whether hon. members opposite realize it or not, I would point out to them just what this means to the western producer. In the three prairie provinces, in which almost all that wheat is produced, the annual provincial budgets amount to $102 million, Saskatchewan's share being $52 million, Alberta $28 million and Manitoba $22 million. In every year from 1943 the marketing of their wheat has cost them a much greater sum than the entire cost of administration of the provincial governments; yet we hear all this controversy

Canadian Wheat Board Act
about taxation problems. That is what this government has taken from the pockets of the western producer of wheat alone, to say nothing of coarse grains and live stock.
Reference has been made to the Oatway case. The courts were denied by order in council the right to proceed with the case in connection with this man's participation certificates from the Canadian wheat board. In the face of all that, surely the government will permit this matter to go before the agriculture committee for further consideration so that we may be in a position to question officials of the board-something that has not been allowed for a good many years.
The Canadian farmer has never received a fair share of the national income from any government in Canada. During the first world war, according to the bureau of statistics, the farmers received about twenty-nine per cent of the national income. During this war, at the peak, they received eighteen per cent of the national income, which I think everyone will agree is most unfair to the primary producers of the country, in comparison particularly with the United States. There the government has guaranteed the agricultural producers at least ninety per cent of parity. During the war years, and for a period of two years following the war, those farmers were receiving for their products thirty per cent above parity, which is vastly different from the condition of our farmers in western Canada.
Something was said about barley and I understand that authority is to be taken in order that the board may handle barley whether they intend to do so or not. In this connection I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of December 4, 1946, entitled "Topsy-turvy Politics":
There is a degree of irony in the official report that the Canadian wheat board has authorized the export, under permit, of a quantity of malting barley to the United Kingdom at a price of $1.80 per bushel. When carrying charges and malting premium are added the actual price, f.o.b. Fort William is $2 per bushel. This barley, it is officially stated, is being sold for human consumption, not for malting purposes.
Nothing could throw into clearer relief the folly of the United Kingdom-Canada agreement, under which for the present and ensuing crop years vve are selling wheat to the United Kingdom for $1.55 per bushel. Fort William. As a food cereal, barley is inferior to wheat. Yet the inferior cereal fetches $2 and the superior cereal $1.55. Indeed, the topsy-turvy, wrong-side-up, policy of the government is worse than this. On a basis of weight-the true food value of cereals-our wheat if priced equally with this barley would fetch $2.52 per bushel.
No doubt the answer that will be offered is that the wheat agreement compensates for the present great losses to our wheat farmers by 83166-40
guaranteeing them better than world prices in the crop years 1948-49 and 1949-50. Such an answer, however, is wishful thinking. The agreement imposes no obligation upon the United Kingdom to make good our present losses in the later years of the agreement, and so to argue is but to seek escape from present criticisms at the gravest risk of international ill-will later on. The United Kingdom government is not bound in any way, shape or form to compensate western wheat growers in later years for the beating they are now taking, and public men who say so are but adding heavily to the ill-service they have already done in signing the wheat agreement.
That is the article from the Winnipeg Free Press.
May I say that I was rather surprised to hear a couple of my friends to the left, both very good and practical farmers, the other day speaking against free enterprise and capitalism. I know that both these gentlemen- one the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough) and the other the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright)-are distinctly free enterprisers. They are both capitalists, and they cannot prove anything else by any dictionary in this land. Yet they went on to speak against the very type of thing they represent.
Maybe that is a question.
The hon. member for Melfort even said that by these controls we have now under the wheat board, agricultural production is decreasing very rapidly; and with that I agree.
It is not right, even if you do agree.
It is not decreasing?
No, not under the wheat board.
The minister has not been out talking to the farmers.
I have not the figures before me.
I have them before me.

If you will refer to pages 159 to 162 of Hansard at which is reported the speech made by the hon. member for Melfort, you will find that he quoted figures from the bureau of statistics which set out exactly the decrease that has been taking place under several items.
I will give you the right figures later.

I pass on from that. Some reference was made to the new agricultural bill in Britain. Much has been quoted about Sir John Orr on food at this particular time. I just want to read from his remarks as

Canadian Wheat Board Act

reported in the Manitoba Co-Operator of January 15. The head note reads: "Sir John Orr Foresees Food as Beachhead for Attacking World Economic Problems", and he is quoted as follows:
Moreover, close government control over production, however necessary it may be in war time, in peace time would end free enterprise for the farmer who . . . would have to produce exactly what he was told to.
Farmers in this country and in the country where I come from-
That is Britain.
-do not relish such a system. What they need is an orderly market at fair prices. They believe they are quite capable of planning their own production for such a market.
He said further:
The farmers of the world outnumber all other workers together and supply the basic needs of mankind.
That is his version of free enterprise right there. I have another article on "Britain Eyes Nationalized Land Trend", but I am not going to quote it. However, it points out that if the farm owner over there now sells his property at anything over the price that he paid in 1939, it goes to the state. It is quite an article. This is what I want to come to about production. In the Searle Index for January 8, 1947-just last month-there is a paragraph under the heading "Farming Under Socialism", which reads:
The British Labour-Socialist government has just brought down legislation which will guarantee to British farmers prices for many crops. The price to be paid by the farmers, themselves, however, is that the government will exercise complete supervision and control over all farming operations. The legislation provides that if any farmer refuses to abide by the official regulations as to what to grow and how to grow it, the farmer may either be imprisoned, heavily fined or, if necessary, may have his farm taken from him. The first case heard was that of a farmer in Lincolnshire, Mr. Balph Bishop, who was sent to prison for four months and tinea $6,000 for sowing six acres more of a crop than the regulations provided. British farmers, therefore, it would seem, are paying a high price in the loss of their independence, liberty and freedom for whatever "price-security" the Labour-Socialist government is giving them.
The Tories did not do so well in the by-elections either.
Will my hon. friend stand up and say that he favours nationalization of land in Canada such as they have in Britain?

If the hon. member will permit me to ask a question I should like to do so. He has travelled all over the world. I want to bring him back home. The simple question is this: Are you in favour of the opening of the grain exchange?

Mr. Speaker, I doubt if there is any member in the House of Commons today whose record is so clear and so frankly stated as that of the hon. member for Souris with respect to the Winnipeg grain exchange. I think that my hon. friend will find that if he will refer to Hansard.
State it now.
You have heard it.
What is it?

When we get into committee on this measure I shall have much more to say. I hope that the minister will refer this matter to the committee on agriculture and colonization, as I asked at the beginning of my remarks, in order that we may have a frank accounting from the Canadian wheat board upon the handling of the producers' products throughout those many years.

Mr. Speaker, I would feel very remiss in my duty as a Manitoba farmer if I did not rise at this time and support such a resolution as this with respect to the Canadian wheat board. Having Canadian welfare and interest at heart, I am sure that I could not do anything else but support legislation like this. In the past I have always supported it, and I shall always continue to support that sort of thing until the produce of our farmers is no longer an object for speculators and profit-seekers to play with, but is rather put in the channels of consumption in the most efficient and economic manner to the benefit of both producers and consumers.
The resolution before the house asks that the same powers now provided by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act be put into this act. The minister in his remarks, to be found at page 591 of Hansard, said:
The bill proposes to provide the government and the Canadian wheat board with more powers than are provided by the present act, but with less power than was provided by order in council.
Well, that is what we have been wanting. I do not see any objection to that. When the minister brings in the bill we shall then know where we are going. There may be something else in this bill that I do not know about, but when he brings the bill down I am then going to read it and find out just what my position is going to be on it. As far as the general tenor of the resolution goes, it is something that I have been fighting for ever since I came to this country, and I hope I shall be successful in the fight to maintain the Canadian wheat board.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
As I said, I am going to take only a couple of minutes to put forward my idea and say that I am supporting this bill. I see that my good friend, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), has gone out. He brought me pretty near home when he began to talk about Britain. Do not rise, Mr. Speaker, because I am going to stay in order. I am not going to get out of order. But might I tell this hon. house that when Robert Burns in his poem said:
See yonder poor, o'erlaboured wight,
So abiect, mean and vile,
Who begs a brother of the earth To give him leave to toil.
-the man he referred to was a tenant farmer. In Britain today ninety per cent of the farmers are tenant farmers. The hon. member did not tell us that. Ask the minister of pensions, whose grandparents were born on a croft in Scotland. Britain is coming to the front today as she never did before. Everybody is up against it, but she is leading the way and I hope God spares me to see her make a success of it, because she will only be coming into what Robert Burns preached two centuries ago. To my hon. friend from Manitoba may I say that I do not quite agree with him. Of course he knows that.
You do in a great many things.

I heard what he said. I have read it in the Winnipeg Free Press and the Prairie Farmer, and the grain exchange have sent me their literature. If he had told me I might have believed him, but I will not believe it coming from the grain exchange. I had the pleasure of visiting Britain a year ago. I met the food minister and the minister of agriculture; I went into the wheat situation and the bacon situation. The farmers of Britain are not complaining, as my hon. friends to the right would make us believe. They are more satisfied today than they have ever been. I shall not say any more, Mr. Speaker, in case you rule me out of order. I am going to support this resolution, and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) does not put into the bill anything to the detriment of the western farmers, I shall support it also.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I do not intend to delay the house for more than a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, but certain things have been said on which I should make some observations. The first matter I should like to refer to is the recent raising of the domestic price of wheat to $1.55 a bushel. I should like to commend the government very much for that action. I may say it is something I have urged for the last year, and something I am 83166-40J
sure will meet with the approval of at least our party in Saskatchewan; I think I can go at least that far.
In regard to the attitude toward the wheat board, and whether or not what we are doing here amounts to socialism, I should like to say this. If there is one thing the farmer has come to think he is entitled to it is the same measure of security that he sees enjoyed by other people in society. He sees, and it has been accepted for many years, the statement made that fair prices should be paid in industry; that there should be minimum wages; that if a person is thrown out of work he may be assured of an income under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and so on. The farmer feels that he has enough to contend with in the possibility of crop failures, and sometimes to a certain extent the failure of markets, without having to face the possibility of having almost to give his crop away. I am one of those who in 1932 sold No. 1 northern wheat for nineteen cents a bushel. That did not even cover the cost of seeding and threshing alone; and the farmers certainly say to the people of this country that they are just as entitled to adequate fixed minimum returns for their labour, which is just as important as any other labour in the whole country, and that they are just as much entitled to fair minimum standards of living as the workingmen or anyone else.
When our opposition friends suggest that any steps taken to bring this about, by some system of the stabilization of markets and prices, and so on, verge on socialism I say they do not do themselves justice. Surely they do not oppose minimum wages. Hon. gentlemen opposite have not opposed a certain measure of protection for industry on the basis, as they say, of giving an assured income to the people employed in industry. Well, if down through the years the farmers of this country have had to pay millions of dollars in higher prices to the protected industries of this country in order to give that protection, surely they are entitled in their turn to protection against the vicissitudes of world markets and so on; and I do not think there can be any objection to that. Certainly I am sure there should not be any objection on the part of the Progressive Conservative party.
I am one with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the suggestion that if the government enters into industrial or commercial activity it should not seek to hide behind any prerogative of the crown as against the subject with which it does business. Any suggestion that the crown should be able to enter into commercial and industrial activities and do what it pleases in regard to

its dealings with an individual; break contracts, as it has done in Saskatchewan, and then hide-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friends may laugh, but they cannot deny it. For a government to do that and then hide behind the prerogative of the crown so that the subject may have no redress I say has no place in a democratic country today. So I say that if our government is going to engage in business, handling wheat or anything of the same nature any subject should have the right to go to the courts and ask them to do justice between him and that commercial enterprise, just as he would have the right if he were dealing with a private individual or corporation. That was what I meant by my interjection during the remarks of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I have heard a great deal from the hon. member's friends out in Saskatchewan to the effect that I talk one way and act another. But I say to them, and they know, that since I have been in the house I have fought just as faithfully and consistently for the farmers as any one of them has.
How did you vote for dollar wheat?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
How did I vote for dollar wheat? That is a favourite, untrue statement that is made out in the west. At the time the motion before the house was for the second reading of a bill to raise the price of wheat from seventy cents to ninety cents. The present premier of Saskatchewan, then sitting in this house, moved that the bill be not read a second time but that we express the opinion that the price should be higher. As I pointed out in the house at that time, and as was admitted by the present leader of the C.C.F. party, if that motion had carried it would have meant leaving the price at seventy cents instead of raising it to ninety cents. The untrue statement is made throughout Saskatchewan that I voted against dollar wheat. I voted for wheat at ninety cents rather than seventy cents, and the people who voted for the motion voted in effect to leave the price at seventy cents. That cannot be denied.
May I just go on with this question that has been raised by the opposition. I think all hon. members will agree that we do not want to get this matter of the handling of wheat and the carrying out of our contract with Great Britain into a condition of chaos such as occurred, for example, in another country when controls lapsed by reason of the

fact that the legislature did not act in time. The powers under which we are able to carry out our agreement with Great Britain and handle this whole question of wheat in an orderly way lapse at the end of March as hon. members know. So I would say this to them. If this matter goes to committee is there any guarantee that it will not be held there so long that these powers will lapse? Once it has gone to committee, no one can be sure that it will be reported back in time to be passed by this parliament before the powers lapse. So I say, do not jeopardize this whole situation by saying this particular bill should be referred to committee, just because you want to look into the activities of the wheat board. Those activities can be looked into at any time by the agriculture and colonization committee; or, if there is any real demand for it, a special committee can be set up. I am sure no Liberal government would say that any body of men handling an important part of the business of this country should not be subject to check by parliament or, if parliament sees fit, by a committee of this house. But you do not have to endanger this bill and run the risk of throwing this whole situation into a state of chaos by insisting that the matter be referred to that committee. There can be such an investigation without having this bill referred. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, I am so anxious to see this programme carried on in an orderly fashion, and it is one which is in the best interests of the farmers of this country, particularly those of western Canada, that I do not think the suggestion that the matter be referred to a committee should be pressed.
I believe, however, that any crown corporation engaging in industrial or commercial activities on behalf of the government should lay i-ts operations before a committee of the house, and should do so as a matter of course. This is done today in respect of the activities of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, officers of both organizations appearing before committees of the house. Therefore I am sure no one would object to the activities of the wheat board being laid before a committee of the house, and considered thoroughly. But that matter should not be mixed in with this debate.
Something has been said as to this agreement not being in the best interests of the farmers of the west. I shall not take long to discuss the point, or to do more than to say that if it were not in the best interests of western farmers I do not believe it would have received the endorsation, of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. That is an organ-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
ization with the ability to look into 'the alleged disadvantages in the agreement, in the same way as hon. members who now criticize it. But apparently they feel that, on balance, the agreement is in the best interests of the farmers of Canada, and for that reason they definitely endorse it. If the representatives of the farmers think the agreement is in the best interests of the farmers of Canada, then I think we may safely take it for granted that the agreement is good for us.
But here is something I have often wondered about. I have seen members of the C.C.F. repeatedly rise in the house, as they have done today in respect of this measure, and endorse what the government has done. I have heard them say that the government is doing what is best for the people, and I have heard them attack the Progressive Conservative party because it has opposed' what we are doing. That is the attitude taken by the C.C.F. time after time in the House of Commons. But when they go out on the hustings in Saskatchewan members of the Liberal party are described by them as the tools of the vested interests, the hired servants of the big interests in the east.
I should like to see a little more sincerity in the speeches made by C.C.F. members in the west. I should like to hear them making the same speeches out west that they make here in the House of Commons, when they praise the government. If they did so, they would sound more sincere.
Mr. Speaker would rule it out of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I have heard members from other parts of Canada applauding what the C.C.F. members say on the floor of the house. They come to me after and say, "Oh, they are not such bad fellows." But I say to them, "Just listen to them when they are out west on the hustings."
You have to defend the Liberal government out west.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have not heard you defending them much. Of course you may be different from the kind of C.C.F.'ers we have in Saskatchewan. If you do any defending of the Liberal government, then I have yet to see your type in Saskatchewan. I am afraid that if you did that in Saskatchewan you would be thrown out of the party. Others have been, and I warn you to be careful.
I shall conclude by saying that the basic idea behind the wheat agreement is that the farmer should have some stability of income; I think everyone will be in agreement with that. I do not think it is necessary to take
rigid control of everything the farmer produces on his farm in order to give him the security which he is getting by this measure.
I suggest that one of the basic ideas behind the wheat agreement is the fact-and I should like to make it as clear as I can, because this may be the last time I may speak in the house on this question-that there is provision in the agreement whereby, when it comes to fixing the price for the crops of 1948-49 and 1949-50, if we have supplied wheat from the crops of 1946-47 and 1947-48 to Great Britain at a price lower than she would have had to pay for it on the world markets, that factor will be taken into consideration in the fixing of the price for the last two years of the agreement.,
I know the suggestion has been made that the British people are hard traders; but that does not mean a thing. The farmers of western Canada understand-and I am in agreement with them on this-that when the British people made this agreement they took into consideration the fact that they might be getting wheat cheaper in 1946-47 and 1947-48, and that if they got such wheat cheaper than the world price that fact would be taken into consideration when fixing the price for the last two years of the agreement. I, for one, believe that they will live up to their agreement. I believe this means that, although we may be taking less today, as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) said, it means that in the last two years of the agreement, relying upon the word of the British people we shall get more than we otherwise would.
To say, therefore, that the farmer necessarily is losing because he is selling for less than the world price, and that he is necessarily losing that much, is to suggest that one does not believe the British will live up to their agreement. I believe they will. I believe that the government of Canada will see to it that the farmers, not wishing to take the last cent from consumers in these days when there is so much starvation and want, will not suffer loss in the days ahead. The farmers of Canada, by taking a far-sighted view, and by not insisting upon getting the last cent in the present time of crisis, will receive consideration for that action. In the long run, over a period of years it will be found that the leadership being given to the farmers of Canada by the outstanding farm leaders who have asked the farmers to take this farsighted view, has been good leadership; it will be found that they followed along the lines of true statesmanship; and that the government, accepting their advice, also acted along the lines of true statesmanship and as true friends of the farmers of Canada.

The points to which I shall refer in connection with the resolution have to do with the charges which allege that the C.C.F. advocate controlling the farmers to death. I do not think that is the real issue. The issue is, are we or are we not in favour of the orderly marketing of farm products? I think that is the principle of the resolution, and that principle we are supporting. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) who, I regret, is not in his seat at the moment, in his anxiety to throw something at the C.C.F. went to some lengths this afternoon to try to prove something that is not so. Apparently they are not afraid of state guidance and planned economy at election time, however fearful they may be about it today. This resolution is a most important one; it is in that class of things which, if it is not possible to cure them, may have to be endured. A question was asked as to the visible supply of Canadian wheat. On February 7, 1947, the visible supply of Canadian wheat was 129,700,000 bushels.
A question was asked regarding quotas on authorized acreages. There should be no doubt as to the position, in regard to marketing quotas on authorized acreages. In announcing the government's wheat policy on July 30, 1946, I stated:
In connection with deliveries there was, of course, no restriction on ,1945-46 deliveries, and it is the intention of the government to instruct the Canadian wheat board to accept all the wheat that producers wish to deliver in 1946-47. The best information we can get indicates a continued over-all world shortage of wheat and wheat flour in the coming year. Deliveries in the last three years of the pool will depend upon conditions of production and of markets. It will be provided in the new orders that the deliverable quantities will be determined by the governor in council before each new crop year, but in any event, the deliverable quantity shall not be less than 14 bushels per authorized acre. The latter provision should safeguard wheat producers against an extreme reduction in deliverable amounts, should the available markets be smaller than we expect.
During the discussions of the United Kingdom contract during the last session I stated, Hansard 1946, page 4846 that the authorized acreage in the prairie provinces stands at about 22,000,000 acres. The actual figure at the present- time is 22,100,000 acres. The position, is therefore as follows: There is no restriction on deliveries for the present crop year. For 1947-48, 1948-49 and 1949-50 producers are assured of deliveries of at least 14 bushels per authorized acre. I need not add of course that -if markets continue to be available in good volume there will be no restriction on wheat deliveries in any year during the contract-.
You intend to continue the power to have the restrictions if you feel they are necessary?

If it is necessary. It is hoped that all wheat offered will be taken. The minimum of fourteen bushels an acre will enable us to see that there is an equitable marketing of wheat in the event of a very heavy crop.

The fact is -then that you are keeping the power to accept as little as fourteen bushels on- 22,000,000 acres. It is the question of j"our power I am asking about. You are continuing to keep that power?
That will appear from the bill.
