Another question was asked regarding participation certificates. In announcing the government's wheat policy on July 30. 1946, I stated:
After the ten cent payment on the 1945 crop has been made-to bring the initial payment up to $1.35-the plan is to place the remaining surplus from that crop in a five-year pool with the succeeding four crops of 1946, 1947. 1948 and 1949. Participation certificates will be issued in the usual way, but payment on these certificates will not be made until after the conclusion of the five-year pool at July 31, 1950.
In other words, the deliveries of all five years will be bulked in one pool with the same initial price of $1.35 ruling throughout the period and the surplus resulting from the marketing of these crops will constitute the participation payments.

In connection with that statement, may I ask the minister whether, in the bill which he proposes to bring down, the policy is to be continued of paying no participation certificates until the end of the five-year period? Is that policy to be continued in the measure to be brought down?
Yes, it is.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to the wheat board, although I do not know whether this is the time to ask it or not. I have received, as perhaps other members have also, quite a voluminous correspondence regarding whether or not the wheat board is eventually to terminate its operations. I do not know how this has arisen. There must have been a rumour somewhere. Perhaps it went over the air. Perhaps some speaker at some farmers' convention made a suggestion. I do not know what happened, but it was peculiar to me that suddenly I received three or four letters one day, three or four letters another until the pile became rather high, asking me whether or not the wheat board was going to terminate its operation. My reply was something like this, that because of the present wheat contract it appeared as if it were necessary for the wheat board to continue its operations at least until around 1950, so that I did not think there was any reason for alarm, but that I could not, of course, foretell what the government's wheat policy might be in 1950. Would the minister make some statement that would set at ease the minds of our farmers who are anxious for the continuance of the wheat board and fear that the government is going to change its policy?

The bill that will be before the house will clearly show the position of the wheat board for the next few years and what will happen at the termination of
the United Kingdom contract. However, I can assure the hon. member that it is the intention-and that is why this legislation is before the house-to have the Canadian wheat board continue.
I should like to ask the minister what policy on participation the government proposes to follow under the new act with reference to wheat marketed in other provinces such as Ontario and Quebec.

No decision has been arrived at regarding policies on wheat grown outside the designated areas, those designated areas being western Canada and certain parts of British Columbia. If it is decided to operate a pool in any other part of Canada during the life of this contract it will be a one-year pool.

In order that there may not be any misunderstanding with regard to the question I asked a few moments ago, may I read from the Alberta "Wheat Pool Budget" of January 31, 1947, the following under the heading, "Will take all wheat":
The Canadian government, through the wheat board, will take all deliveries of wheat up to July 31, 1950. This statement was made by Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, while addressing the annual convention of the United Farmers of Alberta, in replying to a question from one of the audience.
Hitherto the understanding has been that the only guarantee the government would make with regard to deliveries of wheat was the acceptance of a minimum of fourteen bushels per authorized acre. The authorized acreage in western Canada is around 22 million, which would imply the acceptance of 308 million bushels in a single crop year. Mr. Gardiner said that in some years marketing quotas might be required throughout, but in the end the government would accept all wheat marketed in the five-year period ending July 31, 1950.
This is the official publication of the Alberta wheat pool. If the members of the pool who were at that convention understood anything different, then I cannot see why this should have been allowed to go out. I might say that a similar statement was made in the newspapers in western Canada immediately after the convention.

The statement which has just been read corrects what was said all over western Canada. It was said all over western Canada that, under the order in council as it was, there could not be more than fourteen bushels to the acre delivered. A member in that meeting got up and asked for a correction of that, and I corrected it much in the words of this report, which was not submitted to me before it was printed but which, nevertheless, to all intents and purposes does give
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the explanation which was given. The explanation was that what the order in council said -I am not saying what the bill is going to say because the bill is not before the house- was that quotas could be established1 by the wheat board, but in no year could the quota established be less than fourteen bushels to the acre. They might establish more but they could not establish less; and I made it clear to them that was the position and is the position now. I did not say what the position is going to be other than that I expected that it would be somewhat similar to what it is now.
In dealing with the future, I made it clear that in the years when a limitation was imposed, we had from 200 million to 600 million bushels of grain stored in our elevators and a limit had to be put on deliveries under the quota system in order to make it possible for everyone to get some wheat into the elevators. In other words, it was stated here this afternoon that there was a certain number of bushels of wheat marketed in one year and a greater number marketed in another year. The reason for that was that there was no place to deliver the entire crop of wheat in 1942, with the result that we had 600 million bushels of wheat stored in our elevators and much on the farms. Therefore we said to the farmers that they could deliver first only five bushels to the acre, then ten bushels to the acre, and so on, and finally reach the point where we could not take in any more. I said that, in my opinion, that condition would not arise under this agreement, that there was very little if any possibility of the condition arising, while this agreement is in existence, where there would be a blocking of our elevators because the world was not prepared to take our wheat; and because of that I did not expect that under this regulation, if it continued as order in council or however it continued, the wheat board or anyone else would limit the deliveries of wheat. In reporting the matter to the house, the minister indicated that there would have to be some very unusual circumstances arise before any limitation would be placed on delivery. Therefore in my opinion, and I still hold that opinion, by the end of the three-year period it will be possible to take delivery of all the wheat; and if it is possible, it will be taken. As a matter of fact I have said in the house before, and I say it again now, that there is not any authority in this country that could stop the delivery of wheat if there is any place to deliver it. Every hon. member knows that and knows the reason for it.

I brought this matter up just in order to clarify it, because it is indefinite. The second paragraph in the article said:
Hitherto the understanding has been that the only guarantee the government would make with regard tq deliveries of wheat was the acceptance of a minimum of fourteen bushels per authorized acre.
The first two lines of the statement read:
The Canadian government, through the wheat board, will take all deliveries of wheat up to July 31, 1950.
The minister gave you a guarantee a little while ago that it would be utilized only if conditions such as I have described arose, and said that those conditions were not likely to arise.

Then I do not see very much justice in this acceptance. At the present time prices of wheat on the world market are high and farmers are allowed to deliver all the wheat they can. In the latter part, of the period, when I think the government and most of the farmers of western Canada believe the price of wheat will be down, they may be allowed to deliver only a 14-bushel quota under certain conditions at the guaranteed price of $1.35.
Would my hon. friend suggest that the quota provision be taken out altogether?

The point is this. If on July 31, 1949, the elevators should be plugged so that the government would not be able to take the rest of the wheat that had been growm in that period, nevertheless the government should still undertake to pay $1.35 a bushel for the wheat which might be in the hands of the farmers at that date, to be delivered at a future time. The guarantee we want is that the government will pay $1.35 a bushel for all wheat grown within that period, whether or not it is possible to accept delivery of it. If they will guarantee that the $1.35 will be paid at whatever time the wheat can be accepted by the government, that is the guarantee for which the farmers are asking. Up to date the government has not made it clear whether or not that is the policy.

I am not free to say what is in the bill, because the bill is not before the house. I think I know what is in it, but I believe it would be much better to discuss the questions now being asked when the bill is in the hands of hon. members. I believe that all these points can be cleared up then to the satisfaction of all hon. gentlemen. At the moment, however, I do not feel free to discuss the bill.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

I should like to make it clear that, as far as this group is concerned, we shall bitterly oppose any proposal to limit the price of $1.35 a bushel to less than the total production during the period in question.
You will not oppose it any more strenuously than I will.

I am very glad to hear that we have the support of the Minister of Agriculture; and with the support of the Minister of Trade and Commerce I think we have good reason to hope that this will be the case, especially if the Minister of Justice will also support it.

In reply to the question asked by the minister, I would say that I have no objection whatever to a quota being established in any section of the country or all over the country, if necessary, if the elevators cannot accommodate all the grain that may be hauled. I consider it only fair that the quota should be established, provided that all the wheat is accepted before the end of the contract period.
That is the main part of this provision.
The minister did not answer one or two other questions, and I would ask whether or not he is prepared to do so.
I have another answer.
It was with respect to moneys now held by the government on sales of wheat in excess of payments made to the farmers that I was interested.

This is it; I was just waiting for an opportunity to give this answer to the further question of the leader of the opposition. The question related to the surplus in the hands of the board on January 31, 1947, on the 1946-47 operations. This question cannot be answered, or the reason that the board is in the midst of its 1946-47 operations. I would hazard a guess, however, that the board would not have a surplus on the 1946 crop account as at January 31. The board would 'have a large liability in regard to country stocks, because over seventy-five per cent of the accepted wheat marketings have been delivered by producers. Against this liability only a part of the marketings to diate have been delivered to the board' at the lakehead or at the Pacific coast and have been subject to sale. As the crop year progresses, the board will reach a surplus position. This is inevitable with a fixed initial price of $1.35 a bushel, while 160,000,000 bushels are being sold to the
United Kingdom at $1.55 a bushel plus carrying charges, with about half the domestic requirements being sold on the same basis, and a substantial quantity of wheat being sold as wheat or as flour to a wide range of countries at the board's class 2 price, which up to date has ranged from $2.05 a bushel to $2.49 a bushel.
I would not hazard a guess as to the final surplus on the 1946-47 crop account. It will depend upon the course of world wheat prices for the remainder of the crop year and the rate at which the railways can move the remainder of the 1946-47 wheat deliveries. There were otheT questions, but I do not think they refer to this bill.
From what the minister has said I gather that the wheat board has paid the wheat growers $1.35 a bushel for more wheat than it has received payment for?
That is the answer.
Therefore at the moment there is no surplus in this account?
That is right,
I can very well understand how that may be the position. The minister rather hesitates to make an estimate as to what the surplus of money will be at the end of the crop year.
Yes.
Would he venture a guess as to whether it would be less or more than $100,000,000?
Well, I have discussed that point with the officials of the wheat board, and they do not care to hazard a guess.

It is quite obvious that at a certain period it will be a very substantial sum. It must be. Could the minister tell the committee what rate of interest the board receives on that money as surplus, or how the money is handled?
I have just explained that up to the first of the year there was no surplus. When a surplus does exist the rate of interest obtained varies up to three per cent.
When there is a surplus is it deposited in the banks? Is that the policy of the board?

It is temporarily
deposited in the bank and then invested in proper securities.

During the debate on the resolution, the hon. member for Lake Centre made a ugorous attack on the wheat board.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I do not think it was justified. Listening to the hon. member, I thought he cast doubt, if not suspicion, on the operations of that board. Then he proceeded to say that we in this group were opposed to having the statement of the wheat board referred to a committee of the house. I want to correct that statement. In 1942, 1943 and, in fact, at every session I have asked that the statement of the wheat board be referred to the agriculture committee. Now I would ask the minister if he would be prepared to say that those statements of the wheat board which have not already been submitted to a committee of the house will be submitted to the agriculture committee this session. If that point were cleared up, I believe it would straighten out the minds of many people as to whether or not this bill should be referred to the committee.

I was going to make a statement on that point, but I thought the matter was pretty well covered by the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern. I can say that the operations of the wheat board for 1945-46 have been compiled and are being audited. When that is completed I shall lay the report on the table of the house and ask that it be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization.
The report for 1944-45 has ne\ er been placed before that committee. Will the two reports be forwarded to it?
We are agreeable to having it considered at that time.
Can we not go through all the reports we did not consider during the war years? Did the hon. member for Melfort get all the information he wanted in those other committees?
Yes, I got everything I asked for.
The reports for 1944-45 and 1945-46 were not before the committee. They can be dealt with.
If I understood correctly, in the measure to be brought forward, the minister intends that power will be given to assume control over the marketing of coarse grains-oats and barley. Is that correct?
When the bill is submitted the leader of the opposition will see that it provides for certain powers in connection with coarse grains, giving authority to the board to deal in them.

Then the answer is yes. Mr. MacKINNON: Yes.
fMr. Wright.]

In answer to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe I understood the minister to say that surplus money, or money not paid out to farmers from the sale of wheat, was invested in the bank, in proper securities.
My answer was that it was placed temporarily in the bank, and then invested in proper securities, such as government bonds.
Does the wheat board invest in securities funds received from the sale of wheat? It seems to me that those funds should be payable back to the farmers.
Those funds will be paid, just as soon as it is possible to pay them. In the meantime, however, for the benefit of the farmer-producer, we are getting the best possible interest.
Did the minister place any of it on the stock market?

The minister has answered fairly the question I asked respecting moneys received from the sales so far made of the 1946 crop. Can he advise the committee how much money the wheat board is holding now in respect of crops of previous years, which moneys have not been paid out on participation certificates?
That information is not now available-
I would not expect it to be, immediately.
-but I shall consider the question of the leader of the opposition.

In replying to the question of the leader of the opposition, would the minister give a list of the securities held, and the rate of exchange the wheat board receives on the money lying in the bank from previous years?

The policy of the wheat board is to invest any surplus funds from time to time in proper securities, and on the advice of the Bank of Canada. I am sure that when the operations of the wheat board for the last crop year are being considered by the committee on agriculture, that question could be answered in detail.

Would the minister undertake to give those details as to the securities now held by the wheat board, and the interest paid by the bank to the wheat board on moneys not invested? I should think the Bank of Canada would give advice as good as could be given by any other bank, and I should think these would be selected securities. I

Canada Grain Act
can see no reason why the house should not have a list of the securities held by the wheat board, and the interest paid by the banks on moneys not invested in securities.

I do not know any reason why that information should not be given. My ansrwer was that it would be given when the accounts of the board are before the committee on agriculture, and before that, if possible.

I was left in some uncertainty as to the minister's statement respecting the government's policy in relation to the wheat of Ontario, Quebec or the eastern provinces.
I understood him to say that he had not yet reached a decision on policy. May we take that as an intimation that there may be some change or amendment, in order to define a policy in respect of wheat in these other districts?

Ontario-grown wheat has been handled under a certain policy for this year. That will be continued until June 30, the end of the year. Some time between now and June consideration will have to be given to the policy for the next year.
Then we are to understand that the marketing of Ontario wheat is under a year-to-year policy?
Yes.
The marketing of western wheat is under a five-year policy?
Yes, that is right.

The effect of the price on Ontario wheat would be considerable, and from year to year alterations could be made? The Ontario wheat grower is at the mercy of the whims of the government, which changes its policy from time to time, and writes a new policy each year. Is that not correct?

I think that is exactly what the Ontario growers want. But we are dealing with t-wo different matters when we consider western wheat and Ontario wheat. This bill to a great extent deals with wheat grown in the designated areas.
But it affects the price of the wheat grown by Ontario farmers. The Ontario farmer takes fifty cents less and may not get it, while the western farmer takes fifty cents less and hopes to get it.
As I said earlier today, the Ontario farmer gets $1.40, as against $1.35 advance received by the western farmer.
Did I understand the minister to say that some sales of wheat had been made at prices at high as $2.49 a bushel.
That is wheat or flour.
Some sales have been made at prices as high as that?
Yes.
During this crop year?
Within the last few days.
May we have copies of the bill?

Immediately, I understand.

Postal Service
Hon. ERNEST BERTRAND (Postmaster General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 17, respecting supplemental payments on mail contracts.

I wish to say a few words about the additional payments which the minister is permitted to make to mail couriers. The general effect of that provision is that the Postmaster General may at the end of one year, if in his judgment the contract has been let at too low a figure, adjust the contract upward, and for succeeding years he may then fix such additional amounts. I believe that the whole principle is bad. One may go into any other field of human endeavour-and I agree that these things are let by tender-and if he accepts a tender to do so-and-so at a price which is too low he necessarily bears his loss. That truth is the whole virtue of doing things by tender.
If I read this bill correctly, if a man has tendered and receives a courier's contract, as some hon. member called it, at too low a figure, he can come back and say, "I took it at too low a figure." It is then adjusted upward and will continue on that basis. In other words, there is no yearly tender which would overcome the whole difficulty.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the Postmaster General would do this, but it may happen. We will assume that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and I applied for a mail contract-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member
would not get it.

That is the brightest remark the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) ever made. Let us assume this simple fact. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) applied for a contract, and to spread the thing out widely we will say that his bid was $1,000. I applied for the same contract and my bid was $800, and I was therefore the lowest tenderer. Looking at the two of us, I am sure that the Postmaster General would try to give me the contract even though my tender may have been higher than the other, but we shall leave that out, and assume that it is done on the basis of the amount of money that it is going to cost the country. My bid is accepted and I have the contract. Then at the end of one year I go to the Postmaster General and say to him, "I tendered much too low; I lost money on this contract." I suggest to him that he raise my contract, and being such a kindly disposed person, naturally he would raise the
contract and he would no doubt make it $1,200. I would then carry on from year to year on the basis of $1,200. I know it is infra dig- if I may use that legal expression-to talk politics in this chamber; but let us assume that t'he present Postmaster General were not there; that some minister who knew something about patronage took his place. A simple thing could happen-

We never
know; that may happen.

I have no ambition in the world other than to be the Postmaster General of Canada. I am a bit lazy; I do not like to work very hard. Let us assume that a postmaster general took the place of the hon. gentleman. That postmaster general may be just a little bit politically inclined, and a mail contract was coming up. The politically minded gentleman who was the postmaster general might be the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The hon. member for Souris puts in his bid of $1,000 and I put in my bid of $800. I am a friend of the politically minded postmaster general; I come back in a year and have my contract raised to $1,000 or $1,001 or $1,200, and I so continue. My point is this; that will be the simplest way in the world of exercising political patronage. May I at once absolve myself of making any accusation of that kind against the present incumbent of the office because I am not doing so; but I am perfectly certain that if I were the postmaster general I would protect myself against even the suspicion of a charge of that kind.
With respect, sir, I ask reconsideration _ of the section because of the invidious position in which the highest minded man in the world can put himself. I know that when some of us are speaking politically we say what per-, haps pleases our own side most. I thought I heard someone to my left say "hear, hear", and I was about to say, in response to that, that they know exactly what I am talking about, but that is neither here nor there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do not put words in our mouths; we were silent for once.
The hon. gentleman asks me not to put words in his mouth. I will not do that but it might be of great assistance to him at some time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is very good.

My definite and serious suggestion is-and I would make it irrespective of whether the party over there were in power or we were in power or any of the other groups to my left were in power, and I mean it equally-do not do it. I consider it
Postal Service

unfair; it is unwise to put any minister in that position. I think I may say, in fairness to this government, that they think they are open to attack in a number of legitimate places. The attack that I speak of may be illegitimate and yet a lot of people would believe it.
I suggest to the minister that he leave this whole thing on the basis of tender, without assuming and absorbing a lot of punishment which probably would not be coming to him but which he will inevitably get the minute he raises contracts. People will say, "Of course he did it for A. He was a friend. He did not do it for B because he was not a friend." With great respect, sir, I suggest that that section should be altered or deleted from the bill.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): There is another phase of the same question with which the minister must be familiar. A number of mail contracts have expired. In the ordinary course, tenders have been called, and the department over which the Postmaster General presides has declined to enter into contracts because it considered that all the tenders, even the lowest, were too high. That has happened a number of times. I mean tenders for the same service have been called more than once. The result is that the carrier has been asked to continue on an indefinite understanding as to both the duration of his contract and the remuneration he is to receive for his services. That, I submit, is a thoroughly unbusinesslike way of carrying on the government's affairs, and it tends to deteriorate the service and to create dissatisfaction and suspicion among those who are carrying and those who would carry the mail.
The reason advanced by the minister for what I consider an objectionable provision in the bill, the provision to which the hon. member for Calgary West has just referred, is a compelling reason for accepting the lowest of the tenders that have been called for, and it would be enlightening to me and possibly to many other members of the house if, in the course of his remarks, the minister could say how many rural mail contracts have lapsed in the last year and how many times tenders have been called and received and none accepted. I understand that the number is considerable. Would the minister give his attention to this phase of the matter when he is discussing the appropriate clause in the bill?

The hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson) is unavoidably absent tonight, quite a delegation 
from his riding being in the city, but I know that were he here, he would have something to say, because, after listening to the minister the other night, he remarked to some of us about some cases in his own part of the province.
I believe the minister said that the rate of remuneration paid to letter carriers in the country could be raised by himself, as this bill calls for; and the minister made the statement that certain letter carriers had had their remuneration increased because they had asked for it, owing to war conditions, I suppose, and other reasons. The hon. member for Durham pointed out that if a letter carrier too humble to ask for the increase had not applied for it he would not get it. He put that question to the minister and the answer was that such a letter carrier would not receive it. I cannot put my hand on the minister's statement but he remarked in effect at the time that, unless letter carriers asked for the increase, they would not get it. In the opinion of the hon. member for Durham, it is altogether unfair to letter carriers, of whom there are a number in his riding, to say that, if they do not ask for the increase, they will not get it.
There are no rural routes in my riding although there are delivery men, but I agree with the hon. member for Durham that, if the minister raises the rate for a letter carrier on one route, because the increase has been asked for, it is not fair to the letter carrier on the next route, merely because he is diffident about asking for the increase, to withhold it from him. I hope that, when the minister rises to speak, he will clarify that position. It does not sound reasonable or sensible to me.

I would not support this bill if it were of a permanent nature, but it is a temporary measure to take care of a situation that has arisen during the war, and we hope that the minister will be able to bring in for the next session a policy which we shall be able to support. Subsection 2 of section 3 of the bill might not be altogether fair to some of the carriers who are not close to large centres, being more or less in settlements on the outskirts. It is provided that payments under a mail contract shall not be supplemented under this section unless the person entitled to payment under the contract makes a written application. I submit that notice should have been sent out to all the carriers so that they would all have had an opportunity to take advantage of this provision. I know of several cases where they are getting a pitifully small pay,

Postal Service
and they did not know until recently that they could have a bonus if they made application for it and if the application were allowed.
I should think it would be possible for the department to work out a schedule of rates that could be paid to full-time carriers. For instance, if the carrier were working full time on pavement, there could be a settlement for that pavement per mile, and in the schedule the department could take care of different kinds of road such as gravel road, dirt road, or prairie or bush trail. It would be practicable to work out such a schedule for these carriers working on a full-time basis, but in the case of the carrier working only part time we shall have to get back to the old system of calling for tenders.
I differentiate between the full-time carrier and the man who works only part time. We are all agreed that the full-time carrier should have a rate of pay which he knows he will receive and does not have to apply for, and that rate can be fixed in accordance with a schedule of the kind I have mentioned. Moreover, the carriers should come under the civil service commission and be able to receive the benefits which accrue to civil servants in the form of pension and so forth.
These are just a few suggestions, and I hope that the department will be able to devise a policy that will give our postal carriers a better deal and a measure of security.

I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for The Battlefords so far as subsection 2 of section 3 is concerned. In some of the areas with which I am familiar, outside of the larger urban centres, men do not have the opportunity, and the postmasters are sometimes not so alert in acquainting these rural delivery men with all the provisions of the postal regulations. I think the point raised by the hon. member is timely.
Speaking more particularly with regard to subsection 2 of section 3, I think the minister should devise some plan to make sure that every carrier has this opportunity and is acquainted with the regulations. I also wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) in what he said about the advertisement contracts. Recently in my district-and I have brought this particular case to the attention of the minister-I believe there was an instance where a contract had been advertised two or three times and still the most unsatisfactory service is being attempted to be given on this particular route. It seems to me that some means ought to be devised whereby the constituents on the route could be better protected. In the instance I have in mind, the situation has prevailed for
some time. I know the people on that route at the present time are getting most unsatisfactory service. Someone advised me

I believe it was the superintendent-that it is being advertised again, and I understand that on the 28th of this month it will be allocated to someone. It seems to me that there ought to be some way by which these rural people could have a satisfactory service and not be subject to the unpleasant circumstances that develop in connection with contracts such as those to which the hon. member for Stanstead referred to, and which I can confirm from my own experience.
There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer, and it was touched on by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). Going back over the years I can recall clearly an instance where there was a definite suspicion that the very thing referred to by the hon. member for Calgary West actually happened. I was familiar with the circumstances and I feel quite satisfied that such did happen. Therefore I believe that the minister ought to put some provision in the bill in order to protect himself in the proper way.
As a final suggestion-and I overlooked mentioning this before-in this arrangement to supplement contracts which had been made does the minister not feel that, before he makes an award, protection might also be given by providing in this bill that he will again call for tenders before he makes an increased award? I say that advisedly, because I have seen the operations of this thing for quite some time. I suggest to him that he embody in the bill something requiring that another tender be called for. Then, if satisfactory tenders cannot be obtained, I would not object to having the minister, particularly the present one, make the award that he thinks is fair and reasonable. In that way the people on these routes would not have their services disturbed, and yet no suspicion would creep in that something had been done a little bit under cover. With these few suggestions, I am quite willing to allow the bill to go through second reading and to be dealt with on the separate clauses.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it my dutyr to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) on this bill. As an hon. member on the opposite side said a few moments ago, this bill is not of a permanent nature and gives the minister powers to deal with a situation of emergency that arose out of the war. As far as my district is concerned, it is true that many routes are now without carriers. The public interest is deeply concerned in this matter because, if
Postal Service

the minister has not any authority to pay out moneys provided for a subsidy in order to level out the situation, a bad situation may develop for the carriers and more particularly for the people in general. In my riding, I have one of those instances in which the carrier gave up the route, for good reasons, I suppose, and does not carry out his duties. There are about sixty-two constituents on this rural route who have not received their mail for more than two months because the Postmaster General has not the power, as the law now stands, to enter into a temporary agreement with this carrier. Consequently this route is without any carrier at all. I understand that there is a proverb used in my riding to the effect that when one wishes some misfortune to befall his neighbour, he wishes him to become a Tory, or to get a stepmother, or to get a mail contract.

I think in all fairness we should give the government, and more particularly the Postmaster General, in order to meet this dire and acute situation, the same powers as exist in his department as far as these contracts are concerned. I have no hesitation at all in giving my support to this bill, because I know that the hon. member who is at the head of this department will do his duty in all fairness to every carrier concerned. Subsection 4 of section 3 reads:
No supplemental payments shall be authorized under this act later than sixty days after the commencement of the next session of parliament following the coming into force of this act.
That is the kind of protection I like and approve. I do not know why the house should not give this bill its unanimous support, because it is in the public interest that the situation which now exists in the department should be corrected as soon as possible.

I wish to say just a word to the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) in regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). Where the department advertises for tenders-and the minister has already indicated that he considers this a proper and fair method-and the tenders received are considered too high, I understand that in some cases the department will notify the former carrier, the man who previously had the con-

tract, suggesting that he renew the contract at a figure lower than that of his tender, while in other cases the department will call for tenders a second time.
I should like the minister to explain this. Where the department has advertised for tenders; the officials consider the tenders too high, and the former contractor is invited to accept the tender at a lower figure, I should like to know what investigation is made or what basis is used to arrive at the figure suggested by the department. It seems to me that the contractor, who knows the route and knows the conditions, is certainly in the best possible position to arrive at a reasonable figure, instead of being advised by the department at Ottawa that the tender is too high and that he should accept a much lower figure. So that when the minister speaks I should be glad if he would give some indication as to whether that is a common practice, and some idea of the number of contracts handled in that manner.

I am very much in accord with a good many of the principles of this bill, which has been introduced by the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) to rectify a condition which, over the years, has grown up in my constituency and my province and, I suppose, all over Canada. It has been the duty of the department, when the four-year period was up and a mail contract terminated, to relet the contract to the same carrier, if he would accept it, rather than allow it to go up for tender; and I assume that some of these low figures which have been and are being paid to mail contractors refer to contracts that have been carried on for perhaps ten, twelve or fifteen years. These were carried on until the war began; then, rather than upset the whole rural mail system and call for tenders all over again, the Postmaster General saw tit to give bonuses on some of these smaller contracts.
Of course I live in the banana belt, where we have good roads and our mail contractors are smiling, pleasant fellows. I have read over all the contracts in my constituency, I believe, and I could not see that there was anything but great fairness on the part of the Postmaster General in the amount of the bonuses he has given. He has practically standarized the contracts in my part of the country at about $40 a mile.
Since this matter has come up, and since that letter went out last fall, it has been my privilege to get in touch with a good many of our rural mail carriers. I remember one, a friend of mine from Oil Springs, who has a mail route of 27-5 miles. About eight years

Postal Service
ago he tendered for that route at $875. He could do it at that figure in those days because then you could buy four or five gallons of gasoline for a dollar; you could buy a set of tires for much less than you have to pay today, and you could operate an automobile for much less. When the war came along, however, he found that he could not drive 27-5 miles a day, 300 days in the year, for $875, and he was given a war bonus of $225, which brought his contract up to approximately $1,100, or very close to $40 a mile. His contract ran out a year ago. We took up the matter with the Postmaster General, who did not wish to open it to tender again, and who gave this contractor the assurance that, if he would accept the contract at $875, he would still be given the bonus of $225 for practically a year, but he could not assure this tenderer that the full $1,100 would be paid during the term of the contract. I got in touch with that young gentleman, and he said he could do it, and do a good job. He is quite well satisfied at $40 a mile; and when any definite figure is being considered I would suggest that probably $40 a mile might be taken as an over-all figure. Most of those to whom I have spoken about the matter are quite well satisfied with this figure.
There is another matter I should like to bring up. I believe that when a mail contract is terminated and tenders are called, the age and physical condition of those tendering should be taken into consideration. I know of one contractor who is eighty-eight years of age. About the beginning of the year, he tendered again and got the contract. He never intended to carry it out. He wanted to get it in his name so that, after a month or so, he could transfer it to a friend of his. At the same time, there was in that neighbourhood a young veteran, a farmer boy, who had a very bad leg, so that he could not carry on the heavy and arduous duties of farm life. He would like to have obtained the contract, but he was not a particular friend of this old gentleman. Therefore I suggest to the Postmaster General that when a contract runs out, before it is relet, the age and physical fitness of the tenderer should be taken into consideration. I do not believe that anyone over sixty-five years of age should be given a mail contract. I am up in that age group myself; I can speak for the men in that class, and I know I would not want to undertake a mail contract. In any event, when we get through with our new social legislation which will be coming up soon, any man who reaches the age of sixty-five will be taken care of anyway. I just offer that suggestion from my own experience.

Mr. Speaker, I consider that the principle of the bili is wrong and, unless the minister is able to convince me to the contrary, I shall certainly have to vote against it. It seems to me that the whole principle of contracts is being violated. It is being left wide open to political skulduggery and deceit. The main thing that strikes me is that, once a contract is entered into, that contract should be lived up to unless it is such a bad contract that it should be cancelled. If a mail contractor has undertaken a contract he is unable to fulfil, then I think the only sensible thing to do is cancel the contract and call for tenders all over again, and, when the new tenders are considered, various considerations should apply. If a man has been giving good service, I believe that should be taken into consideration. Merit should play a great deal in awarding this second contract, and if the contract is being let a second time a competitive price should be considered. That is the only reason contracts are let out by tender: so that a competitive price can be secured. Usually the lowest bid is accepted.
Under the bill, the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) is given authority, even after tenders have been called for and a contract given, to raise the contract price. What will happen to the man who lost his contract because he was a little high in his tender? There is no element of fairness in a provision of that kind. I can see the reasoning, too, in a situation where a man has accepted a contract at too low a figure. To deal honestly in the matter, some consideration should be given that person. He should not be expected to do a day's work-and the carrying of mail is hard work-without receiving sufficient pay.
But the whole situation lends itself not only to political skulduggery but also to deceit. I cannot submit to the principle of the measure because, as was pointed out before, a man can put in a low bid deliberately, and then come back to the Postmaster General and have the bid raised above those of his competitors.
He would be badly caught.

No, he would not be caught, because all he has to do is to send in a written petition giving sufficient reasons. Who is to decide whether those reasons are sufficient? The Postmaster General decides it. I am not implying that he would be deceitful in this respect; but it must be remembered that he is not on the ground. He cannot be all over the country at one time and, under the provisions of this measure, he could easily be misled. He could fail in judgment.
Postal Service

In my view it would be entirely too dangerous to let the provision stand as it is. If there are a number of cases of this kind- and there probably are-I would rather see the contracts cancelled entirely and new tenders called for. Then, after competition and merit are taken into consideration, new contracts could be awarded. The minister may point out that there are so many of these it would be a tremendous task. I do not think it would. If there are a great number of them it shows the inefficiency in the method of awarding the contracts in the first instance. That would not speak well for the Post Office Department. So that, generally speaking, I do not think there are a great many of these contracts which are let unfairly. It seems to me that from the point of view of business and good management it would be better to withdraw the bill and bring it down in some other form.

Mr. Speaker,
this subject has been pretty well covered. However, there are one or two points of which I wish the minister would take note, and to which I would ask a reply at his convenience.
In the first place, I wonder how long it is since these routes have been surveyed. I know the map in my constituency is antiquated. A new highway has been built along the St. Lawrence river and many people have constructed homes adjacent to it. Up to the present time, however, no provision has been made for mail delivery anywhere along that road.
My second point is as to the extension of routes. I believe it is the desire of the department to serve all the people of Canada as well as possible in the matter of mail delivery. Yet in my constituency along many of the routes there are people who, to my way of thinking, should be served, but who are not receiving this service. I fully realize that an extension of a route means an expenditure of more money to the carrier. However, I would ask the minister to give these two matters serious consideration, because if we are to serve some of the people I believe it is important that we should try to serve all the people, if at all possible.

Mr Speaker, I have not taken part in the debate thus far. I am going to support the bill, although it does not go as far as I should like to have it go. The service is not satisfactory in every respect, although I have no complaint with respect to rural mail carriers and letter carriers in my constituency. While there may have been some favouritism in connection with 
the letting of contracts in the first instance, on the whole the postal service is well handled, and those who are responsible for the different routes certainly earn any money they receive. They show great courtesy and give a first-class service to their people.
I do not know what the number of routes is in other constituencies, but I know this service in the county of Cumberland is extensive and most important. We have forty-three rural route contractors, thirteen stage services and twenty-two side services. Under existing conditions, with steadily mounting expenses, I do not think any of these persons who are carrying out this important service are receiving adequate pay for the work they are doing and the equipment they have to use.
I should like to read a paragraph or two from a letter I received lately, because I agree with a statement made in it that the rural mail carriers, having in mind the work they do, are the poorest paid of any of the employees of the Post Office Department The letter states:
You know about the work I have to do-
And I do.
-and what the roads are like, blocked in winter and a foot of mud in the spring, and so rough in the summer that a car does not last long. 1 have to keep up a ear, also three horses for winter and spring. I think you will agree with me when I say I should have 50 dollars per mile or more . . .
And I do agree with that.
I have mentioned my own because you know the conditions and most of the contractors are in about the same position as I am.
What applies to this man would apply to the other carriers. He continues:
We are able to carry on along with our farm, but I think a courier, on these long routes, should have a day's pay without having to work half the night on a farm to help make a living. In regard to the contract system, I consider it very bad. The good contractor, all equipped, costing him a lot, and giving good service, at the end of four years his contract is opened. Some person w'ho could not figure a contract tenders very low, gets the contract, is not financially able to do the job, and the patrons suffer on account of poor mail service. The good contractor is out with his equipment on his hands. The Postmaster General will tell you from the floor of the House of Commons that the contracts go to the lowest bidder, if the bonds are good. This is not always right. I feel the contract system has outlived its usefulness and should be replaced by permanency and a mileage basis of at least $50 per mile. I could go on and cite you many more cases. If you can help rural mail contractors in Canada to get proper pay for the work they do it will go a long way to improve the rural mail service for the people.
I am in agreement with what is stated in this letter.

Postal Service
The Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) made some explanation with respect to the bonuses and lack of bonuses in connection with men operating these routes. I do not understand why some of these services having the same mileage carry substantial bonuses, either wartime or operational, while contractors on other routes are not given any bonus or any allowance. I say they should all be put on the same basis. The Postmaster General, in my opinion, should make a real explanation as to why in these post-war years, with costs increasing, some are favoured with bonuses, while others do not receive them. I think this legislation should deal in equity with all, and the Postmaster General, before this bill goes through should make an explanation as to why this condition should continue to exist, and all carriers should not be given a living allowance having regard to today's costs.

Mr. Speaker, when the resolution came before the house last Wednesday, unfortunately I was out of the chamber and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that I was not in the house. When I heard of that I hurried back here to get on record for fear the papers might say I was absent. Tonight I was called out of the house and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicoI) stated that I was called away again. So I am speaking tonight in order that the papers may know that I am here.
Everyone who spoke on the resolution seemed to agree that the bill should be referred to a special committee where this whole question could be discussed, but it is now apparent that it will not be referred to a committee. I would suggest that that be done another year at all events, because I feel that many things could be done to improve our rural mail delivery, which I consider to be one of the most important services which the Dominion of Canada renders to the Canadian people.
I understand that a five per cent bonus was paid to take care of the gasoline used and that another bonus was paid, provided that the mail drivers applied for it. Many drivers applied for and got the bonus, but many other drivers did not get the bonus simply because they did not apply for it.
Last year, a notice was sent out to the rural mail drivers asking them to return a letter saying whether or not they were willing to accept a mail contract at the original rates, which would mean that they would have to deliver the mail without any bonus.

That is the reason why we had to prepare this legislation, 83166-41
because all those to whom we wrote asking if they were ready to renew their contracts at pre-war prices said that they could not do so, and we had to do something about the matter.

The fact remains that many of the rural mail drivers did not apply for the bonus and therefore did not get any, while those who were wise enough to apply for it got it.
I have already brought to the attention of the minister that, following the notice which was sent out to the mail drivers, a letter was sent telling them to ignore the notice as the bonus would continue to be paid. The Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) stated in the house last Wednesday, as reported at page 352 of Hansard:
These bonuses are about to expire on March 31, unless they are extended by virtue of any new law which might be passed. We think it would be unjust to limit these contracts to the price they carried at the time they were passed, and we wish to include the bonus in the extension of the contract after March 31.
A certain number of these contractors never asked for any increase, and have carried on in that way. Of course we are giving bonuses only to those who did ask.
Apparently those who asked got the bonus and those who did not ask did not get any bonus. Again, if the bonus is continued, apparently it is left to the Postmaster General to say how much the bonus shall be and who shall get it. I do not think that is right, because I suppose those who make the biggest kick will be those who get the bonus. We ought to pay this bonus on a basis that is fair to all, on a mileage basis, if you like, or any other basis that is fair, and not just leave it to be paid to those who apply for it.
If a committee of the house were set up to studj' our rural mail delivery I am sure that much could be done to improve the service. It is a disgrace that His Majesty's mails should be carried through this country in some old car with a sign wired on the back reading "His Majesty's rural mail". I do not think we can be proud of that. A committee might well be set up to consider how the rural mail service in Canada might be improved.

Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length on this measure. The numerous speeches already made by hon. members of this house are proof enough of their high regard for His Majesty's rural mail contractors. This feeling is due, first, to the very important services rendered by these men and also, perhaps, to the fact that they are highly valued electoral agents.

Postal Service
Have you ever had experience in this connection?

No, because I have always been in the ranks of the opposition in this house. Mr. Speaker, I am requested to approve the principle of an increased remuneration for rural mail contractors under certain conditions left to the minister's discretion. For those of us who come from rural constituencies and are cognizant of the troubles of all kinds encountered by rural mail contractors, such as the recent storms, when His Majesty's mail was carried and delivered on time, it would be illogical and indecent to oppose the bill. I am, therefore, among those wrho will vote for the bill.
A while ago someone mentioned patronage. In some quarters the fear has been expressed that there might be some form of patronage. Those who are familiar with the work of the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) know-we might as well admit the truth-that the Post Office department is the one where petty patronage is most in evidence, and that is the most distasteful form of patronage that can be dispensed by a minister. Personally, I think that no one can be perfect, and as long as human nature remains what it is and political customs do not change, patronage will never be completely eliminated. Why should we delude ourselves about that? We can only ask the hon. the minister to dispense patronage intelligently.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, *while my name does not officially appear on the patronage list because I am not recognized as an orthodox liberal, my only request to the minister is that he should continue to deal more graciously and even more kindly than he has done in the past with the rural mail contractors in the constituency of Argenteuil.
