Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my word of appreciation and thanks and also bring to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) the efficient manner in which my rural mail has been delivered on Vancouver island and the courteous manner in which his couriers have rendered every possible service that they could to me.
My constituency is covered by a great many rural routes and the conditions of these routes vary tremendously. In some cases it is a fulltime job; in other cases it is only a parttime job. In some cases the couriers are
|Mr. Heon.]
restricted to carrying mail; in other cases they can carry passengers and freight if they have space; but there is one condition which prevails over every route, namely, the great increase in the number of boxes which are now being established on all routes because of the general influx of population into rural Vancouver island. I could cite innumerable instances. I have one before me, a route thirty-five miles long which contained 250 boxes. An additional twenty-five boxes have been added during the last six months.
I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General that, if bonuses are to be paid, perhaps one of the conditions which would earn a bonus would be an increase in the number of boxes which have to be served, because quite obviously the costs go up. The more stops that have to be made, the more mail that has to be handled is a change in the original terms of the contract.
I suggest that a review should be made of the means of distributing the mail to some of the outlying points. I shall cite only one instance, the village of Port Renfrew, which gets a mail delivery once in every ten days by Canadian Pacific steamer. There is now a bus service into Port Renfrew three times a week, and naturally the inhabitants of that area wonder why they can get their mail only once in every ten days when perhaps an alternative route would enable them to get the mail two or three times a week.
I was surprised to learn that the Post Office Department is not required to advertise mail contracts when they expire. If they consider the rate of payment is reasonable and the service being rendered satisfactory the department can renew the mail contract under such circumstances without submitting it to a new tender. I understand that that is correct. That is the statement I have from one of the senior officers of the Post Office Department.
Finally, I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) that consideration be given to placing the full-time rural mail courier on a civil service basis with all the rights and privileges of a civil servant in so far as hours of work, holidays and pensions are concerned.

The rural mail courier problem has been an issue long since under consideration by the department and on different occasions by the house. I realize that it was never more desirable that we curtail expenditures rather than increase them.

Hear, hear.

Postal Service

The minister says, "hear, hear". I am glad the voice of the government is beginning to talk in that way, even though they practise extravagance in many respects.
In view of the important place the rural mail courier has in the public service of the dominion, I could not vote against the evident desire to bring about something closer to equality with other services as is indicated by this measure. Every hon. member and the country have appreciated the splendid service given by the mail couriers, but they have felt for a long time that the system under which they serve the public has become long since outmoded. I am disappointed that the Postmaster General has not seen fit to work out some other plan by which he can give these people reasonable remuneration, instead of the measure which is now before us. A review of policy in that regard is long since overdue.
I realize that this matter has been discussed in the house on many occasions during the last few years. The inequality of the pay of these men has been much more emphasized during recent years. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, or any hon. member who knows rural mail couriers do not feel any great degree of pride when you see His Majesty's rural mail coming down the road. You can tell it without a sign, usually by the clatter of the car, an old, tired, worn-out horse or the rattle of the buggy. The mail courier endures hardships in difficult periods of the year. It is an arduous service; it is a responsible service. If the mail courier is not operating efficiently not only is he certainly subjected to the criticism of his patrons and the citizens throughout the country, but the Postmaster General and his department clamp down on him speedily, and they must do so in order to maintain the service to the high degree of efficiency which has been maintained over the years.
I believe that the competitive principle which has been mentioned here tonight is only going to be aggravated by this bill. Probably the minister does not think so. I know he will agree with me when I draw to his attention the fact that he is going to be allpowerful. I expect that he will increase the rate of every mail courier in Dufferin-Simcoe, because he has always been most kind to me and he knows they are about the most underpaid couriers of any place in Canada. He will have that privilege, but I wish to point out to him that it will not relieve the competitive feature of the present mail courier and the hazard of his job. The present Postmaster General or one from our party, which may be in power after another election, will be up 83166-41J
against this problem. The rural mail courier will know that the Postmaster General is able to increase the rate-
Change "may be" to "will be".
This law is for one year only.
I understand that. There must be a degree of uncertainty in the Postmaster General's mind when he does not make it any longer than that.
No.

Even that is long enough. I wish to point out that that which is supposed to be for one year only is often, by precedents, carried on for many years. Mr. Jones may be carrying the mail on a rural mail route. He is probably a veteran of the first great war and may have some physical disability, a heart condition, or something else which prevents him from taking hard work. Probably he has been carrying the mail for several years. Then somebody who does not understand the difficulties of his task, does not understand that his roads are worse than roads in some other district, underbids him. He says to himself, "Oh, they have passed a new act; they have amended the act; I will underbid the mail courier by two or three hundred dollars. I know a member of the House of Commons who happens to be on the Liberal side of the house, and he stands in pretty well with the Postmaster General. I will go down and get the Postmaster General to increase that rate." The Postmaster General may say that he would not stoop to anything like that.

This law will be in effect for only one year. After one year the Postmaster General will not be able to increase any contract which has been bid too low. If what the hon. gentleman said a moment ago comes about and there is some other postmaster general in office I shall be sorry for that poor postmaster general because he will not be able to do what the hon. gentleman has in mind.

Well, Mr. Speaker, time
brings great changes and we might find another postmaster general assuming as great powers as the present Postmaster General proposes to exercise under this bill because, under the bill, he can give the rural mail carrier anything he likes. He can revise the contract if it is too low. But it does not add to the man's security. Will the Postmaster General tell us now that he intends this for
Postal Service

only one year? Does it mean that the increases are for only one year? Will they be reduced after one year?
I would remind the hon. member that the house is not in committee and questions cannot be put to the minister at the present stage.

I appreciate that, Mr. Speaker. Probably the Postmaster General has been interrupting me more than I have been questioning him. However, I think he is fair and I am sure he is sympathetic, at least to many mail carriers. I would therefore urge that he and his department give careful consideration to the revamping of the whole system of rural mail carrying in Canada.
I do not believe there is any service that is rendered more efficiently and courteously, nor is there any service that is more underpaid. Can one conceive what the situation would be in the civil service if jobs were held on a competitive basis as these jobs are-and, by the way, there seems to be a greater number of jobs every day. Can one imagine the insecurity which these men have to put up with while giving the service they do? The eivil service should be the backbone of the country's administration, as it is in old England. We have in Canada a Civil Service Act and a Civil Service Superannuation Act, and yet for this particular class of service there is no security. A man may sell his farm because he is unfit for that type of physical labour and, when he takes a contract for delivering mail, he must be prepared to bid lower than anyone else. No matter how tow he takes a contract, he has to carry it out; and, after three or four years, when his horse and buggy and his automobile, when he can operate it, are all worn out, then someone else may bid even five dollars lower than he does and the courier loses his position.
Can one conceive of any such situation in any of the departments in Ottawa? What would you say, Mr. Speaker, if some man in my riding could come here and tender for a job at $50 a year less? Would he get it? I urge on the government the most serious consideration of this whole question, because it is something that transcends party politics. It is vital to the service of the dominion, and it is only fair to those who have been carrying our mails that they be put on a secure basis. _
This is something that we have discussed in this house on many occasions in the past, and I realize, of course, that the minister faces some difficulty in trying to carry out the suggestion which has been made by cer-

tain members that he should pay $50 a mile across the dominion. I have talked with other postmasters general in the past and with officials in the department, and I know there are many difficulties to be considered. There are districts where one could not get mail carriers at the rate of $50 a mile and others where one could get them for less. Surely, however, a system could be inaugurated to take the place of this outmoded plan. Just as we have customs officers in certain districts, we could have mail carriers in their respective districts on some comparable basis.
I know there are some routes that are difficult. There are bad roads in the winter and in the spring and fall, while there are other places that' are served by good roads. Again, in places near an industrial area where wages are high it would be impossible to get anyone to take the job at the same rate that might be paid 250 miles away. I suggest, however, that a new policy be inaugurated in this important branch of the government service. I am glad that the minister has expressed the fear that he will not be able to put this proposal into effect for more than one year. It. is a sort of shotgun prescription for an emergency and not a permanent policy, and it indicates that the minister is doubtful about the policy which he is at present administering. Sooner or later I hope that he will give our rural mail carriers at least equality with other public servants.

I should not like this opportunity to pass without saying a word on the question of rural mail carriers, because I have received many complaints from my part of the country. There is so much difference between one section and another that it is hard to standardize mail carriers even in one county. It is hardly fair to expect the minister to know the exact amount of bonus that should be paid in each case, or the supplementary payment that should be made, because even in a single county there are varying conditions. I do not speak for any other part of the country, but in my own constituency there are sections where we get twice as much snow as in others, and naturally it is worth a lot more to carry the mail there because of the bad roads with which the carriers have to contend.
I am not like the hon. member for Lambton-Kent; I do not live in the banana belt. We have in parts of Huron as much snow as one finds anywhere in the dominion, not all the time, of course, but most of the time, and it is difficult to maintain the service. Had it not been for the fact that a bonus was given or a supplementary payment made, many of these carriers in the war years would have quit.

Postal Service
Someone has said that many of these men are too timid to ask for relief. One chap whom I know very well came to me when he received a letter stating that the bonus would be cut off. He wanted to carry on for fear he would lose his contract. But I asked him what was the use of his working for nothing. I said I certainly would not carry my contract if I could not get the bonus. He would not be making money at the job; he would be working for nothing. A man is worthy of his hire, no matter whom he works for and carrying mail is a responsible job and calls for good citizenship. I hope the minister will give this matter his careful consideration.
I do not think the minister should be saddled with the responsibility of having to say what each of the carriers should receive, but in consultation with his advisers he should see to it that these men are fairly treated in all sections of the country, because I do not think it is possible to strike an average. Sometimes I wonder if there could not be some floor set on a mileage rate on rural routes, and then, when dealing with a section where there are bad roads and a great deal of snow, if that standard could not be raised, or some system like that adopted. The system now in effect is unsatisfactory. I will grant you that the contracts of many of these men are their own responsibility. They made the contracts too low. After they had been carrying the mail for a short time, they found they could not do so at the figure in the contract. Then they come back to members of parliament and those responsible for the administration and try to have the contracts raised, when it -was their own fault in the first place that they were too low. But, after all is said and done, I think the carriers are responsible men and should be paid for the work they are doing.

Mr. Speaker, I came to this house in 1940 after the winter election, the one which has been called by many the surprise election because it came as a surprise to everybody who had talked about having an election and did not believe it would come and about the people having no confidence in the government. In any event, in 1940 we fought a long election campaign in the winter, and I had to cover the snowbound constituency of Bellechasse. I had to cover thousands of miles- not in a day, of course-in the two months of the election campaign. I had occasion quite often to meet on the road the rural mail carrier who was going from one point to another in his little sleigh drawn by an old horse and who was, as many hon. members
have said, very much underpaid for the hard work he was doing. To reassure my hon. friends opposite, I may say that the rural mail carriers did not want to take the candidates as passengers, because they feared that, if they took a Liberal candidate or a Conservative candidate, in the event that either party won it might hurt them afterwards. The result was that I had to furnish my own means of locomotion, which was sometimes by snowmobile and sometimes by sleigh. I can assure you, sir, that the mail carriers could not afford a snowmobile, being paid, as they were, in such a scandalous manner. However, this is not the fault of this or any one previous government but is the result of practices that have been carried on from year to year and from one government to another; I1 refer to the tender system under which is developed the practice of people underbidding one another to perform a public service for a sum of money that nobody would accept for one-third of the work that has to be done; afterwards they have to make sacrifices in order to carry out properly the duty entailed, and, on most occasions under great hardships on account of the weather.
On many occasions this question has come before the house, and public-spirited members have proposed this or that scheme to improve the lot of the rural mail carrier. We have had these proposals from both sides, and I think we competed with one another on all sides of the house in making them. Everybody expressed the intention of being fair to the rural mail carriers. It is a matter that could be left out of party politics entirely.
One of the most promising measures that was introduced in this house, or that sounded most promising, was brought in by the then member for Wellington South, Hon. Mr. Guthrie. He made the very sound proposal to revert to a system of so much per mile, depending on the hardships encountered or on the difficulties because of the condition of the roads. But he stopped short as most other people have when they brought this question before the house when it came to the method of selecting these mail carriers. He stopped short in his proposal and could not find a solution of how to appoint these people to carry on that public duty; and I think that is the hard point in the problem. Hon. members have all stated that it was necessary to improve the lot of the mail carriers, but no one on either side of the house has yet suggested a practical and just way of appointing them. How can you go about the appointment of a mail carrier by the civil service commission? Can you ask a man
Postal Service

who is going to carry mail to try an examination? Will you appoint him because he has a better-looking horse, a stronger-looking horse or a faster car than some other man in the community? What is to be the criterion which the department will use in appointing a man through the civil service commission? It would be the ideal thing if mail carriers in the rural districts could be appointed on a permanent basis as is done in the cities. That would be quite right. But what education will they be expected to have? What will be the basis of judgment for the department? It is one of the hardest things to determine in order to do it justly. As it is at the moment, many of the associations would like to have those who are now appointed made permanent; then, when they retire, they would like the successors to be appointed by the civil service. But nobody has yet suggested what qualifications will be necessary for a man to have in order to carry mail from the station to the village post office. That has always been the drawback.
I have gone quite rapidly tonight through some of the old Hansards because I had read about this before, but I have not found in the three or four proposals that were brought before the house the correct answer to the problem. Everybody has stated that the mail carriers were underpaid and scandalously underpaid. I might take just a few moments to quote from Mr. Guthrie's speech of April 16, 1929, in which he said:
I suppose that lack of experience has something to do with the unsatisfactory conditions which attended the first tenders and the first contracts, but as time has gone on, conditions instead of improving have gradually become worse until today we find a system established throughout practically the whole length and breadth of this country under which certain men who are practically employees of this government and of this country, for the purpose of carrying His Majesty's mails, are not receiving an adequate return for the services they perform. Indeed, so inadequate is the return to our rural mail couriers that the matter has become nothing less than a public scandal.
In a certain district of Ontario, as quoted by Mr. Guthrie, the mail carriers were getting $40 a mile over the year. Well, in our districts in Quebec it has taken the war and pressure to bring the rate from $20 to $40, while now in other parts of the country where there is even less snow it is much higher than it is at the moment in Quebec. I do not blame anybody for that. If our people are silly enough to underbid one another and quote too low a figure, it is not the fault of any other province. But the fact is that the people are underpaid, and we must find a system whereby we can remedy the situation.

Another proposal brought forward a few years later, in 1936, by my predecessor in this house for the constituency of Bellechasse would not be acceptable, I think, to many who consider that these men should come under the civil service. Mr. Boulanger at the time introduced a bill proposing that the then postmaster general was to award to whomsoever he deemed proper, contracts for the transportation of mail up to the amount of $1,000 per year, and that the contractors should be paid according to a fixed rate per mile per day established by the postmaster general according to conditions and circumstances. At that time, in 1936, he was fixing an amount not lower than thirty-five cents and not over seventy cents per mile per day unless so otherwise authorized by the governor in council. But he left the then postmaster general or his officials as the sole judges of who should be selected or to whom the contract should go. There was considerable merit in this proposal, but I doubt if it would be acceptable to the house.
The measure now before t'he house is one way of trying to repair, shall I say, an injustice to certain people, which is caused not especially by the government but rather by a system and by the people themselves, because if in a certain village they agreed with one another that they should not underbid, they might get a better price. Yet if they ask a little more than the average price for the district, even though for the same type of country in another province the rate is twice as much, the officials of the department come along and say, "No; this is much 'higher than the average for this district," and they ask for more tenders until they find someone willing to take it at a cut rate.
As an example, a chap in my constituency had a contract at $35 per mile per year. His route was very long; I believe the total amount of the contract was about $1,300. He could not make both ends meet at that price and asked for an increase. At that time this bill was not contemplated. His application was refused; they told him it was not possible, so he let the contract go to tender. Well, a man in the same district put in a tender at $1,100. He cannot do the work and make any moneyr. During the summer time he can barely operate his car and figure out a small depreciation, while in the winter he will ruin a horse or two over the long route he has to travel every day. So I, like other hon. members, cannot feel that any of t'he systems proposed up to t'he present is perfect. I 'believe permanent appointments should be the ultimate aim, but in that case how can we judge as to the qualifications of those applying? It is

Postal Service
certain, however, that we should have a per mile basis for each 'type of road in the country or each district, according to whether or not it is snowbound1 part of the year, because the man who tenders receives the same amount when he carries mail in the good days of summer and when he endures the hardships of winter. I believe a minimum of some sort should be established so that at least these people will have a decent living.
I believe this bill should commend itself to *hon. members, because it does aim at correcting the present situation, though perhaps in an awkward way. It is not perfect; no perfect system has been- recommended even during this discussion, or by the officials who have been working on the matter, who are of no party and who have no ambition to please either the left or the right. They have not found a perfect system either. I believe the proposed measure will bring about some kind of relief, and I think we can trust the officials of the department. I do not always like the decisions .they give in my cases, but generally I think they are fair people working not in the interests of any one party but in the interests of the country as a whole. So that I think they may be trusted to avoid abuses and carry on under this bill, as they have carried on previously, in trying to improve the service.

I should like to say a word in support of these mail carriers, who are inadequately paid. I know of one route in my section of the country forty and a half miles long for which the carrier receives $850 a year. Sometimes he has to get through snow ten feet deep, and often he cannot get through at all. That amount is altogether inadequate for the work he does.
I am going to support this bill. I believe the payments should be adjusted upward so that these carriers may receive what they are entitled to. After those adjustments are made, I believe the only businesslike way to let these routes is by tender, because one man is as good as another. I also believe that any returned soldier, either of the first war or of the last war, should receive the preference in the letting of these tenders, because he may be unable to work, and if he can get a mail route he will be able to earn a living for himself and his family.
I do not care to take up any more of the time of the house, but conclude simply by saying that I intend to support this bill.
I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker; there has been too much talk so far.
Carried.
I know hon. gentlemen opposite would like to hear me.
More than your own party do sometimes.

For once the opposition agree with me. Everyone is in favour of something being done for the rural mail carriers. For once I agree with my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). In any legislation the minister brings down we would ask that the carriers of the province of British Columbia be treated exactly the same as those of the province of Quebec.
Better.

At the risk of repetition I wish to say one thing; that is, that I am entirely in favour of continuing the bonus on the mail contracts provided for in the order in council passed under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. But being in favour of one section, namely section 4-and I refer to that only to make myself perfectly clear

and being in favour of the assurance of a fair and proper return for the mail carriers, I cannot accept the principle contained in this bill of placing the minister in the position of being able to determine how the expenditure of several hundred thousand dollars shall be made, that determination to be based upon his opinion that the public interest will be promoted thereby. I have before me Durell on "The Principles and Practice of the System of Control over Parliamentary Grants". I have gone through that book as well as I could. I can find no record of any instance where a minister ever asked parliament to give him the blanket right to expend hundreds of thousands of dollars, whether for a period of one year or less, his position to be uncontrolled by parliament and to be determined only by the question of the public interest.
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) mentioned his difficulties during an election campaign. If, perchance, this should be an election year-and sometimes, having regard to the legislation before the house, one wonders whether or not it is-what a power is going to be placed in the hands of the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) to dispense beneficence, to distribute funds under a blanket order, the determination to be based on the public interest. In a case like that, the public interest is very apt to be synonymous with political interest.
As far as section 3 is concerned, I am unalterably opposed to parliament granting any minister the blanket right of a blank
Postal Service

cheque, to be expended by him in such a way as he shall determine, free of any responsibility to parliament. I quote from page 2 of Durell, where he is referring to our democratic system, and where he says:
The bedrock on which the English system is built is the principle of the maintenance by parliament of control over the grants which it makes. It is one of the old standing principles of our constitution that the House of Commons should control the finances of the country. That is the right, privilege, and duty of the house. It has been achieved by means of struggles lasting through centuries, beginning from tile fourteenth century down to the seventeenth century, when it was fully confirmed, and since then it has never been practically disputed. The cardinal principle on which the whole of our financial system is based is that of parliamentary control, and by this is understood not the control of parliament in its constitutional sense as composed of sovereigns, lords and commons, but by the Commons alone.
Sir, there is no excuse for parliament to grant this power.
What do you suggest as an alternative?

That is a very proper question. I suggest that, if the present rates are too low-and I believe in most cases they are'-then, grant the bonus to all, and place all in the same position.
Here is the position of affairs. There are 4,034 contracts in respect of which bonuses have been granted between March 1, 1943 and December 31, 1946. There are 4,164 contracts, as I understand it, where bonus has not been granted because it has never been asked for. It came as a surprise to me, and certainly to those who haul the mail in my constituency, that there was any provision for the granting of bonuses. They were never made aware of the fact. Those 4,164 are not receiving bonuses today because they never asked for it. Yet we are going to place the minister in a position of being able to determine who of these shall be in receipt of his beneficence and who shall be in receipt of favoritism. That certainly will creep in, however fairly the minister may desire to administer this.
Blanket powers to a minister in a parliament which is endeavouring to regain its power! I am opposed to that. I want to see the mail man receive what is proper and due. Grant him a bonus; grant them all the bonus. But do not place us in a position of having granted a minister the right to determine at his discretion who shall and who shall not receive these additional amounts. That is a dangerous principle. As I look over this book on parliamentary grants, I have endeavoured to find one example-just one-in all the history of British parliamentary government,

but I have been unable to do so. When the minister replies, to sum up the debate, I challenge him to give us one example where any minister has been placed in a position by parliament in Canada to favour one and to deny the other moneys passed in blanket form by parliament.
I shall support section 4 and I refer to it only because I want to make myself clear. I shall support the granting of the bonus to all contractors, in view of the fact that apparently they are all operating at such a low level as to be unfair to both their interests and those of the country. But I deny the right of any minister to have handed to him three or four or five or six or eight hundred thousand dollars to dispense at his discretion, to be determined, not upon a basis of fairness or right, but the basis of public policy and public interest. Public interest and public policy, when the expenditure of money is placed in the hands of a minister, tend to become, as I said before, political interest and political consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in respect of bonuses, but I do not agree with him in his statement as to the merits of the other sections.
The hon. member has said that the bill will give too much power to the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand). All will admit that, during the war, mail carriers were not properly paid and that the government did not give them the money to which they were entitled. As a principle of justice, is it not now a just procedure to have legislation passed to pay back these mail carriers the money they should have received during the war?
These people contributed their war effort; they made sacrifices, but they were not justly paid. All will admit that. In many places when they were receiving $25 a mile to cany the mail they were not receiving adequate compensation. It is only a matter of justice and right that they should be given the money to which they were entitled.
Someone asks: Why not ask for tenders? I say that, if tenders are asked for, we shall not compensate those who have made sacrifices during the war and who, in some instances, did their job for nearly nothing. The purpose of the bill is to render justice to those to whom it is due, to compensate those who suffered and wrho made sacrifices during the war. Others could not have been found in the war years to take over these contracts at the same price.

Postal Service
The Postmaster General now tells the House of Commons that these people have made sacrifices and have spent money in the public interest. He asks us to compensate them justly and fairly. Who can do that best? Surely it is not the hon. member for Lake Centre or myself. It is the man in charge of the department, the Postmaster General himself, who must make the adjustments because some of the carriers have received bonuses while others have not. Some received five per cent and others ten per cent. It is the purpose of the bill to give to all a bonus on the same level, and to give compensation for a service performed. These people will not be repaid for the money they lost during the war years, but will now begin to receive a just compensation. It is for this reason we should support the bill.
If this were a permanent provision, to be effective for years to come, the hon. member's contention would probably be right. But the provision is for a special adjustment to repair a past injustice, one brought about, not voluntarily, but through increased living costs and heavier expenses. I am sure there is no other way of compensating these mail carriers. I believe it is impossible to fix a general rate. How can we say that we shall pay $50 a mile in Kamouraska and $75 a mile in Lake Centre? I would not object to receiving the same rate as is received in constituencies of hon. members opposite for the transport of mail. But when only $20 or $25 a mile is received I say it is only fair and just that the minister should have power to adjust that compensation. It is a matter of public interest; it is a matter of justice. It is a question of administration and the one who is in charge of the administration of the postal service is the Postmaster General. I think, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that we should unanimously support this bill.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, I have been listening for some time to the remarks made by members from all the different provinces and, lest you and the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) might consider that the mail couriers in my constituency of Queens are perfectly satisfied with their present remuneration, I think it is my duty to say a few words on their behalf.
The mail couriers in our province are the finest citizens that we have. They are carrying on responsible work, and they have to do this work 310 days out of the year. They are granted two days holidays. Yet all these men are underpaid.
In supporting the resolution and this bill, let me say that I consider that the bill is a means of legalizing the bonuses which have 83166-42
been paid and which are to be paid. But why should we legalize them on the basis of the vast difference between the contracts that now exist? When the bonuses were granted a year or two ago the department must have estimated them on some cost basis and, as far as I can find out in my constituency, they were basing the cost at around $40 a mile We have seventy-eight mail contracts in the constituency of Queens, and of those seventy-eight fewer than ten per cent have received the bonus.
The rate per mile on the different contracts in the constituency of Queens varies from $18 a mile up to $40, some at $55, a few at $74, and one, I think, at $110. I take no objection to even the highest rate, for it is not too high. What I am objecting to is the lack of uniformity throughout the whole constituency.
Let me give a few illustrations of the discriminations that are caused by the present method of tendering. In different places two men tendered on different contracts covering a distance of 8+ miles. I know the routes perfectly well and the conditions are the very same in both. Yet one man gets $47 a mile, while the other man is doing his work in the very same constituency for $35 a mile.
In two other places that I noted in the list, the route to be covered is 18+ miles, covered by horse and cutter in the winter; in the summer, if they can get the luxury of a car they do so. One man gets $650 and the other receives $800.
I have seen another case where two men have practically the same distance to cover. One man covers miles and the other 21 miles. The man covering 21^ miles gets $850, while the man with the 21-mile route gets $1,550.
Would the hon. gentleman give the names and numbers of these routes? Then I shall have the details by tomorrow morning.

I shall give them to the Postmaster General when I have finished. The $1,550 rate works out at only $5 a day. After all, surely, with a horse and buggy in the summer and a horse and cutter in the winter the man and the horse are worth $5 a day for carrying His Majesty's mail. I am taking objection only to the discrimination between these different contracts. If we can have uniformity of remuneration among these contracts-and I hope the Postmaster General will bring legislation for that purpose before the house at an early date-then all our mail couriers will be more or less satisfied.

Postal Service

At the present time I cannot agree with the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Henderson) when he says that his people would be satisfied with a $40 per mile basis. That is not sufficient for the men who do the arduous work of carrying the mail in this country. There can surely be devised in this house some system which will be satisfactory to all. For instance, the contracts could be based on a certain cost per mile, plus the number of boxes to be served, plus an allowance for proper equipment so that we could have standard equipment for all the mail couriers throughout the country. I do not wish to labour this too much because I know that the postmaster general is anxious to reply to the many questions which have been brought before him tonight. But I do wish to say, on behalf of the mail couriers in my constituency, that they are not in all cases satisfied, not nearly satisfied, and I am certain that they are not paid enough.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention
of taking part in this debate and propose to add only a word. But as I listened to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) and, following him, the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Marquis), it seemed to me that it was worth while adding just a word to what has been said.
In the first place, it appears to me that the background of this is rather odd. I have not been able to understand as I listened why it is that some of these bonuses have been paid and some not. It seems an odd procedure that a large number of couriers who are not quite as well informed as others did not get this bonus for the reason that they were not informed and did not write in. That is a curious background for the thing.
But the point I wish to make is this. It seemed to me that the argument made by the hon. member for Lake Centre was absolutely unanswerable. We want to see justice done. Then let us do it here, not leave it for somebody else to do it. There is no difficulty in writing into this act what is to be done to create a fair situation in regard to all these men. Then why not do it? Unless the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) can suggest some difficulty in the way, I see nothing in the world to prevent us from carrying out what the hon. member for Lake Centre has suggested. Surely he is right in saying that the whole idea of granting a substantial sum of money and then leaving it to be dealt with, not by the direction of this house, but in the discretion of the minister, is a most extraordinary proceeding, and surely, unless

there is some overwhelming reason for it, this house should not consider it for one moment.

The speech delivered by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has prompted me to participate in this debate. Parliament should be very careful about passing this type of legislation. It is clearly unfair to the couriers who did not know that special consideration would be given if they made application. There is no question about it that the cost of delivering mail has gone up all across Canada. The Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) should bring in an amendment to the bill providing for an increase of ten per cent, twelve per cent or fifteen per cent across the board. I am sure that we are inviting trouble if, we consent to this sort of legislation.
I should like to remind the house that similar provision was made for compensation to the lieutenant-governors of certain provinces. The Secretary of State (Mr. Gibson) reported that the lieutenant-governors of Nova Scotia and Quebec were given an additional $4,000 a year, the reason being to cover the costs of extraordinary expenses incurred by these lieutenant-governors on account of war conditions. The payment was recommended by the Secretary of State at the request of the Department of Finance. That type of procedure, the selecting of certain lieutenant-governors in certain provinces or the selecting of certain mail couriers in certain communities and giving them additional take-home pay which is denied to others who have exactly the same arguments is establishing a dangerous precedent. I personally would like to support the argument advanced by the hon. member for Lake Centre that section 3 should be dropped and that the Postmaster General should make a recommendation for increases, because hon. members of all parties are agreed that those who have carried His Majesty's mail have been working for next to nothing, and should have additional compensation.

I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) if this bill meant that in the future these contracts would not be put up for competition. The answer was, in effect, that it had been customary to take the contracts on the present basis, with which I quite agree. I have no objection to the compensation which is sought at the present time, but I would say that there is one thing the rural mail couriers are seeking. and that is full recognition as civil servants. That is one thing they' want. They

Postal Service
consider that they should be recognized and granted superannuation in accordance with the Civil Service Act.
Beyond mentioning that, I have very little to add other than to say that I consider- and I think I can speak with some feeling- that rural mail couriers in my riding certainly face tremendous difficulties and hardships in carrying the messages from one part of Canada to the other and from all parts of the world. There is no one more welcome on the back concessions of Canada than the rural mail courier. I certainly hope that due recognition will be paid to him and to his arduous task.
I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that any special consideration which may be getting the attention of those in authority for the rural mail couriers should be brought before parliament and voted here. For the protection of the minister himself, that is a sound position to take.
In my association in the house with the present incumbent of the office of Postmaster General, I have the very highest regard for him, and I would not for one moment 'hesitate to entrust him with the things that I am critical of at the moment. But we all move on. No one knows what the future has in store for any of us, and I consider that the sound position to take is that any consideration which is being given to the rural mail couriers at the present time-and, goodness knows, they are entitled to greater consideration than they have received-should be recommended by the minister to parliament and passed there.

This bill is very simple in itself, and had to be expected after what we had to do during the war. There have been useful suggestions made by the different speakers, and I thank them very much. I should like to be able to accept them all but unfortunately it ds impossible.
In years gone by, there has been a great deal of discussion about rural mail contracts, and the idea of a yardstick has been brought forward many times. About ten years ago, a gentleman by the name of McKinnon organized an association of rural mail contractors. He received $5 from every one of them and came to Ottawa and lobbied every member of parliament at the time. He wanted to change the contracts and to put them on a mileage basis, but I must say that it was found to be absolutely impossible.
In the department there is one officer who is in charge of this special branch of the work, who has been in that position for over twenty-83166-42J
five years. Of course he would be the first one to accept a mileage basis yardstick; but, if hon. members stop for one moment to consider the large number of cases that we have and that most of these contracts are different because of geography, weather, the weight that is to be carried, the roads that are travelled, the mountains, the summer weather, the winter weather; different because some couriers use one automobile the year round and others have to use automobiles, dog sleighs and, at different times snowmobiles and so forth, they will see that it is impossible to have a yardstick. It is almost impossible to have a certain number of them. We would never succeed. The amount that would be paid per mile would be the minimum in all cases. If it were an average it would be unfair to those who have difficult roads, and it would be unfair to the department if it were given on the basis of easy roads. It would mean that in the last instance a large number of people would tender for an easy road, for example, at the minimum price.
Then would come questions of patronage which do not exist today; because, if there were several tenders at $40 a mile, for example, how would the Postmaster General grant the contract and to whom? Of course, in the case of veterans, we could always give the preference to the veteran, and to the veteran who had the best service in the war. But there would be many instances where there would be others besides veterans, instances where there would be no veterans, and it would be a straight case of patronage. When the war broke out it was found, after a while, that we would have to do something to help these poor mail carriers. Now a contract is a contract and there are two ways of looking at the matter. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) said, when a contract is let we should expect the man who has made the contract to fulfil it.
In ordinary times this might be satisfactory. Certainly it is satisfactory if you are dealing with a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or the T. Eaton Company or any other such concern which is well able to carry out its contract even if it loses a considerable sum of money. But it was not possible to apply this principle in this case at the beginning of the war with such a large number of rural mail carriers who generally, it must be admitted, are not rich people. They have to earn their bread from day to day by means of their automobiles, trucks, buggies or dog-sleds.
It was therefore unanimously agreed-I do not recall that there were any critics at the
time-on October 31. 1941, that a cost of
Postal Service

operation bonus of five per cent should be given mail contractors whose rates were established on or before April 29, 1941.
Unanimously agreed by whom?

An order in council was passed and was published and, when I say that there was unanimous agreement, I mean that there was not the slightest criticism. Under the circumstances I think I am justified in saying that it was unanimously agreed to by the House of Commons, although the matter was not specifically discussed in the house. And so everyone received five per cent except those who had not established their contracts on or before April 29, 1941. On March 24, 1942, there was another order in council, P.C. 2310, which was passed amending the previous order in council, in order to clarify the situation and to apply that five per cent to temporary mail contractors, because the Minister of Justice thought at the time that the first order in council applied only to the full-time mail contractors; that is, mail contracts that were not temporary but for the full time, namely, four years. On March 24, 1942, another order in council was passed, P.C. 2311. It empowered the Postmaster General to enter into temporary agreements for the conveyance of mail.
That is where the bill which is being presented today really takes its root. The first order in council was to apply to everyone, but this was a different one. It was an order in council which was absolutely independent of the previous one.
Also unanimously agreed to?

Unanimously agreed to by all those who received the benefit. It was found that the question of fulfilling the contract was becoming very difficult because automobiles were getting older; it *was difficult to procure tires; gasoline has been increased a second time; there was a great fluctuation in the labour market; costs of every kind were going up and there was a scarcity of equipment. Therefore P.C. 2311 was not a general increase to all contractors, because all of them did not ask, and as a matter of fact did not need, to be helped. A large number of contractors were satisfied to carry on their contracts. They had their equipment and were satisfied to make a fair return on their work at that time.
When this order in council was passed granting the extra bonus, were all mail carriers and drivers notified about it?

I do not know
whether all were notified. Legally everyone is notified when the order in council is published according to law.
May I ask the minister another question?
Yes.
Order. I would suggest to the hon. member that he wait until the house is in committee. The minister is not allowed to reply to questions at this stage.
I asked the Postmaster General for permission.
Nevertheless I would suggest that the hon. member wait until we are in committee. That is the proper procedure.
I think I answered the hon. gentleman anyhow. In the legal sense everyone was duly notified and quite a number of them came and asked for the bonus. I shall be able to give the figures.
May I ask a question?
I have already suggested to another hon. member that the proper time for questions is when the house is in committee.

A number of members have asked what the rule was that was used in granting this bonus. The contractors came, of course, to see the officers of the department and said that they could not carry on their contracts any Longer without assistance, and they gave their reasons. The gentleman who is in charge of the matter is an old officer of the department and he knows whether the price was too low or not, because many people were coming and he acquired a large experience. Besides that, quite a number of contracts were becoming extinct, and if the gentlemen did not want to renew, the department had to ask for new tenders. We found at that time that, whenever we were asking for new tenders, these new tenders were at a very much increased cost to the department, because the gentlemen who were tendering were afraid that the cost would continue to rise and they would lose money. That is one of the reasons why this order in council was passed, in order to give a bonus to those who did not want to carry on their contracts. We found, from the statistics, that,, wherever we were asking for tenders, the cost wras much more than it was where we were contracting with the man who had the contract and were giving him a little bonus in order to induce him to keep his contract and carry on. Hon. members will realize that at that time it was very difficult to get the

Postal Service
necessary equipment, and the tenderers were asking a high price in order to cover the possible increased cost of the equipment and so forth. I want to give hon. members a few figures.
During the period beginning January 4, 1946, which is recent, to March 29, 1946, the tender rate-that is, for all the tenders that were accepted during this period-was $274,587; up to June 28, 1946, $507,470; and to September 27, 1946, $833,774. The old rate in the first period, instead of $274,587, was only $206,003; up to June 28, 1946, instead of $507,000, it was $385,000; and up to September 27, 1946, instead of being $833,000, it was only $635,776. That is not a perfect comparison because it does not give the mileage. But, reduced to mileage, it gave from January 4, 1946 to March 29, 1946, an increase of 33 per cent; to June 28, 1946, 32 per cent and, to September 27, 1946, 31 per cent. So that at all times we kept these figures in mind and we realized that, by giving what I would say was a good increase as a bonus, we were still keeping the cost of our contracts below the price asked by tenderers. It was with the knowledge that had been acquired, because quite a number of them were being dealt with, that different amounts were given. I know this is against the ordinary rules that governments have to employ, but we were in extraordinary times. We had to have rural mail carriers to handle the mail; otherwise we would have been short in many places and there would have been greater inconvenience than was experienced.
I gave the figures the other day on the resolution, but I wish to give them again. During the period from March 1, 1943 to December 31, 1946, there were 4,034 contracts where bonuses were awarded at a price of $3,282,412. This is an increase of 36 per cent, and it carries a mileage of 44,244. During the same time we contracted by tender another amount of contracts. From March 1, 1943 to December 31, 1946, 4,164 contracts were awarded, and the new rates brought the contracts to a total price of $3,333,455. That is an increase of 36-6 per cent.
Were those operational or war-time bonuses?

They were both, because the first bonus of five per cent disappeared very fast. When we renewed the contract we gave the second bonus. The first one that disappeared was included in the other one. Those contracts covered a mileage of 44,244 miles. During the same time we contracted by tender for 4,164 contracts, only 130 contracts more than the contracts with
bonuses. The cost of those contracts ran up to $3,333,000, almost $75,000 more than the others. It is true that there were 130 contracts more. The increase on the tenders is 36-6 per cent, but where we find the difference is that these -contracts which cost more than the others, although there are one hundred more, cover only 35,590 miles instead of 44,244 with bonuses. So that it is evident that the contracts with bonuses were more advantageous, to the department at least, than the contracts granted by tender. I may say that they also gave more satisfaction to the contractors because they were asking for help and they preferred to keep their contracts with a little bonus rather than to take the chance of having to tender.
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) asked me if the guarantors are released when the contract is abandoned. I have to admit that is so. In years gone by, these contracts were for four years, with a guarantor who was responsible; if the contractor did not carry out his contract, the guarantor had to carry it out; otherwise he would be liable in damages. Two or three years ago, we found we had difficulty in getting contractors if we did not give them the option of cancelling their contracts on three months' notice. There is now provision in all these contracts that, if the contractors want- to get out of their contracts and get their guarantors out, they can give notice of three months and we will accept that.
Order in council P.C. 2311, passed in March, 1912, was replaced by order in council P.C. 5833, which was simply a clarification of the previous order. The last one, P.C. 4960, was passed on June 17, 1943. The main section of that order in council reads:
That the action taken under the power granted by these orders in council shows that the rates negotiated represent a smaller percentage increase in operation costs than is shown in the cases of tenders invited, and is therefore economically sound.
It has been in operation ever since. When the emergency powers act ceases to have effect, all these bonuses must disappear. We notified our contractors at the time the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson) saw me, and it was almost a catastrophe, because we had all these contractors telling us they did not want to continue their contracts without the bonus. More than that, they did not want to tender anew where that situation prevailed, because they were not sure what it would cost. They came to us through their members of parliament and were all very well received. Last year, when I put through my estimates I said I would try to introduce legislation this
Postal Service

year to take care of these cases. Some of those having contracts with bonuses are willing to renew if we incorporate the bonus; that is covered by subsection 1 of section 3 of the bill. But, as has been said, a certain number of contractors did not ask for the bonus granted by virtue of the last orders in council; some of them were absolutely satisfied to carry on their contracts in that way. Some might have been shy about asking, but I think hon. members will have to admit that it is not for the department to go around and tell these gentlemen who have contracts that, while they do not have an absolute right, they might come and, if they can, prove that their contracts were being carried on for too little, and they would have a chance to get a settlement. Some came; some did not. A certain proportion of these gentlemen are willing to renew their contracts, though we are not giving the bonus any more. We shall only do so if we get the power, but we have not done so for quite a long time, almost a year. In the case of the contractors who want to renew their contracts, we are ready and willing to give them a similar amount, calculated in the same way that we have calculated the bonuses of which we are speaking at the present time.
I can quite understand the attitude of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). I always listen to him with pleasure. I always come in when I know he is going to speak, even when he speaks in favour of a bill of rights, and if I do not agree with him I always enjoy listening to him because he argues like a good lawyer. His only defect is that he goes to excesses in his arguments; he always goes too far. He quoted from a well known author this evening; but, after all, we are only asking the power to renew contracts with bonuses for those who have not such bonuses already, and that for a period of one year, or until sixty days after the opening of the next session. The Postmaster General cannot in any way do wrhat the hon. gentleman has in mind, because there is a section of the act which says that we cannot grant the bonus to a contractor who has not had his contract for more than one year. If I were asking for tenders today, and one man should tender at a very low price of $800 as against perhaps $1,000, hoping that after one year he could ask for $1,200, with a chance of getting it, in no way would I be able to grant that request, because after one year from now. the law will not be in force. Of course, in six months I could grant it to a man who ma3r have had a contract for six months already, but when that man put in his tender six months ago he could not have known that this legislation would fMr. E. Bertrand.]
be introduced. So that there is very little in this bill, and I feel that we are simply rendering justice to these people. It is a temporary arrangement giving the force of law to something which will help us get out of a situation created by the war, and I believe the house might well approve it.

In order to clear up the situation, it would be better if the minister were to answer now. He said that the operational and war-time bonuses were all included in the figures he gave us.
For a certain time. There was a five per cent bonus for increase in cost, and when there was a renewal the second bonus included the bonus of five per cent granted in 1941.

The information before
me shows the facts concerning a man who was receiving $475 and who received a war-time bonus of $50. On what were those bonuses based? Another man with a contract for $560 received $140. That is not equal treatment; they are out of line. Here is another one receiving $575, only $15 more than the man receiving $560, and yet he got $275 as a war-time bonus. On what were those bonuses based? How did the Post Office Department conclude as to how payments should be made? Was it on a mileage basis, or on the contract price?

In mjr explanation I said that there was no definite rule because many of these contractors did not get anything. Some came and asked for a small amount because they wanted to carry on, and were satisfied with that small amount. Generally they asked for a certain amount which would allow them to carry on and to live from their contracts. If I had all the contracts before me, by referring to individual files I would be able to give the reason why the amounts mentioned were granted. But without the information before me I cannot do that.
By the way, it is now eleven o'clock and I would ask that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again tomorrow, so that I may have my officials here to help me.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
